speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to use the remaining minutes I have in this debate in a general way to talk about my home province, Saskatchewan.
The New Democratic Party is often getting hit with the label of not knowing how to manage an economy; that it cannot take care of business. In fact I remember back in 1982 when there was the Allan Blakeney New Democratic government in Saskatchewan. At that time the Tory leader, Grant Devine, said that we could afford to totally mismanage Saskatchewan and still break even.
After 10 years we find that the province is some $15 billion in the hole with something like 400,000 taxpayers. It is a monumental problem. This is by a Tory government that knows how to manage an economy. It has put Saskatchewan so far in the hole that it is going to take many decades for us to recover. It has been left to a New Democratic government to correct that error.
I think that the people of Saskatchewan, if you look at the history, are in good hands. I believe it was Diane Francis or one of the right wing columnists who wrote that back in 1981 the Allan Blakeney government was the best-managed government not just in Canada but in North America. That was from a right wing journalist. The record shows that.

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
Back in 1944 when Tommy Douglas took over Saskatchewan, the province could not borrow money. Tommy Douglas came in and built Saskatchewan to where we were in 1982. Talking about fiscal responsibility, Tommy Douglas wanted to introduce medicare but waited some 17 years until the province could afford to do it. In those days the province did it on its own but it was not done until it could afford to do it.
The New Democratic governments in Saskatchewan certainly come from a background of being sound managers of the economy, very conscious of the economy. It actually galls me that people on the other side of the House and elsewhere say that New Democrats cannot manage an economy.
The Romanow government, faced with a huge debt which makes the national debt pale in comparison on a per capita basis, came in with a budget. In the last year of the Devine regime there was something like a $1 billion deficit. In the first year the Romanow government cut that deficit in half to $500 million. It is cutting the deficit in half this year to $300 million. It will have a balanced budget within three years.
That is already a better record than the federal Tory government has had. I have been in the House for the last five years. Every year I hear the same budget speech that this year our deficit is $32 billion, $34 billion, or $35 billion but next year it is going to be $29 billion and the year after it is going to be $15 billion. I think it was the former Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre, who said three or four years ago in the House that this year we were going to have a deficit of $8 billion. What do we have? We have what I believe is the largest deficit in the history of the country, $35.5 billion.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Check back to 1984. It's not the largest.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
It was not $35.5 billion? The minister announced $35.5 billion. The $35.5 billion deficit, whether it is the largest or the second largest, is not something to be proud of.
Saskatchewan has a government that is cutting the debt not on the backs of ordinary Canadians but with a mind to keeping existing social programs. It is cutting that deficit with a view to causing the least harm to those who can least afford to have harm inflicted upon them.
The approach taken by the Saskatchewan government is different from the one this government has taken. This government has used blackmail. It has used blackmail in the area of the Western Grain Transportation Act, the Crow benefit. What has it done? In 1983 the Liberals took away the Crow rate and put in the Crow benefit. That payment was going to be in perpetuity. To me, perpetuity means a long time and not 10 years.
Last December we lost 10 per cent of the Crow benefit for two years. This year in the budget the finance minister said that we are going to take away in two years 15 per cent of the Crow benefit and after that we are going to take away 20 per cent of the Crow benefit and it is going to remain that way.
However, and this is where the blackmail comes in, the finance minister said if they agree to pay the producer the government will give them back that 10 per cent. That is negotiating with a gun to one's head. The Crow benefit and the Canadian Wheat Board are two of the most fundamental mainstays of agriculture in western Canada today, and this government is tearing them apart.
At the agriculture committee yesterday we were discussing the removal of barley from the Canadian Wheat Board under a continental market dual system. Government members refused to allow representatives of the Canadian Wheat Board to appear in front of the committee. I cannot believe it. They were scheduled to appear, they were on the list but the government said no.
If we were going to dismantle Air Canada we would surely have the chairman of Air Canada in front of the appropriate committee, but the government said no to the Canadian Wheat Board.
What is even more outrageous is that the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board is not going to be allowed to appear in front of the committee either. The advisory committee is a committee made up of farmers who are elected by farmers to advise the Canadian Wheat Board. It is the only elected body in the country that represents farmers with respect to Canadian Wheat Board issues. It is being denied access to appear before the committee.
We are going to have one more committee meeting on this issue. Who are we going to have? They took away the Canadian Wheat Board and they are going to bring
April 30, 1993

in UGG, United Grain Growers. This is a company that agrees whole-heartedly with the government's position.
Who else have we had in front of the committee? We had the Western Barley Growers Association. It is an association that has 214 members and receives 90 per cent of its funding from the government. That is a really unbiased group to bring before the committee. At the same time we are disallowing the Canadian Wheat Board and the advisory committee to the Canadian Wheat Board from appearing before us.
The other thing on this issue is that there have been a number of studies come out but the government has ignored them except for the ones that agree with its position. This is the kind of government that has been inflicted upon us in this country.
If that is called co-operation, if that is called trying to find a consensus, then it is looking at a different dictionary than I look at because nothing is further from the truth. They are heavy-handed tactics.
They are exactly what the finance minister used in his budget address a few days ago by telling people in western Canada that they are going to lose 10 per cent of their Crow benefit, that $72 million is going to be gone unless they do things the government's way, unless they play ball with it.
That is not going to go down very well in Saskatchewan. I can tell the government right now it is going to have an issue on its hands, certainly in the province of Saskatchewan, because I do not think the producers of Saskatchewan are going to buy that.
There was a poll commissioned by the Government of Saskatchewan that showed 88 per cent of the producers in Saskatchewan want to at least have a vote. That has been our position.
Talk about openness, talk about a consensus. Surely to goodness allowing the producers, the members of the Canadian Wheat Board, to have a vote on what should happen to their Wheat Board is only fair.
It is unbelievable that a government can talk about consensus and openness and at the same time come down with the heavy fist and iron glove on the people in the prairies. That is exactly what this government is doing.
Government Orders
The government side is saying we are having a plebiscite because the producer will decide whether he wants to deliver to the Canadian Wheat Board or to the open market.
That is nonsense. What we have under the Canadian Wheat Board is a pooling system so that when people deliver to the Wheat Board they get the average price that was received by the Canadian Wheat Board during the whole year. Studies done in areas where they tried dual marketing systems show that the pooling system will fade away, it will fail. That is because during times when prices are higher, if the spot price is higher in the U.S., the Canadian Wheat Board will not receive any grain. If the price is low the grain will come to the Canadian Wheat Board. The only time the Wheat Board will have grain is when the price is very low.
To say that is a plebiscite is nonsense. The other factor is that in the government's so-called thorough study of this issue it has not done any study of the effects of the Canadian Wheat Board in a dual marketing system and the impact on the Canadian Wheat Board. That has not been studied.
The same holds true for the Western Grain Transportation Act. For the finance minister to stand up in this House and blackmail producers in western Canada is outrageous.
The other point is that the grain transportation system in this country is responsible for thousands of jobs, probably tens of thousands of jobs, and hundreds of millions of dollars to the Canadian economy. If we do not produce a strong Canadian transportation system we are going to lose those jobs in the ports and rail crews and in rural Saskatchewan.

Madam Speaker, I listened with great interest to my hon. friend pontificate on the wonderful job the Saskatchewan government has done in cutting spending. I would like to ask him a question directly. Since he is so impressed with the spending cuts of the Saskatchewan government, including closing hospitals and so on, doing what it feels must be done, why have he and his party voted against every single spending cut proposed by the federal government in trying to get its deficit under control?

April 30, 1993
Government Orders

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, the answer lies in the way that governments are cutting. It is true that these days as a social democratic party it is very difficult to implement many of the things that we as social democrats would like to see implemented and maintained. It has been very difficult. Certainly when the government in Saskatchewan is having to cut back in the areas of social welfare, health care and so on it is hard to do. However that is the reality we face.
The minister will know better than I that there is a big difference between a province managing its economy and the federal government doing so. The federal government has many more economic levers than a provincial government. The interest rate is controlled by the federal government. There are a number of levers the federal government has at its disposal which a provincial government does not.
The Saskatchewan government and many other provincial governments find themselves on a precipice. We have had transfer payments to the provinces cut back at an unprecedented rate. Thank goodness there were no transfer cuts this time. That is very much appreciated. However the minister will know that Saskatchewan does not have the economic levers the federal government does. We also do not have the room to manoeuvre in Saskatchewan that this government does. We have something like a $15 billion debt. We have interest rates in Saskatchewan of over $800 million a year and there are something like 400,000 taxpayers. The province only has 950,000 people in it.
It is a very tight situation. What the finance minister, Janice MacKinnon, has done in Saskatchewan, and I know the minister agrees, is to say that if we do not make cuts now we are going to lose our social programs. It is also true on the federal side. We have to get the deficit down federally. This government has been tinkering at the edges. We have had a deficit of over $30 billion every year since this government has been in place. I agree we have to make cuts. We have to lower the deficit, but we have to do it in a way that will benefit all of us and not hurt those who can least afford it. [DOT]
That is the attitude the Saskatchewan government is taking. That is the attitude this government should be taking. There are other areas where this government could be cutting: the $6 billion helicopter purchase that will take place.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Is it $6 billion? It keeps going up.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
I believe with inflation it is going to be $6 billion or $5.8 billion. The government is saying that it can either repair the helicopters or buy new ones. It has that choice. The government is buying 50 helicopters. It is not saying that it could buy those helicopters without the anti-submarine equipment on them. I do not know the exact figures but that alone would save billions of dollars. Some 35 of those helicopters are going to be able to chase submarines attacking this continent. The old Soviet subs are rusting in port. It should send over a tourist to take a photograph of them so that it would know where they all are instead of spending that kind of money on anti-submarine equipment.
That is an area where the government could cut. That is an area where it would get support from this caucus. If it came in with a plan showing that it would keep helicopters for search and rescue, that would be great. However I do not think we need the extra equipment, the sophisticate computers and so on that are designed to attack submarines. There is a whole host of added equipment on them. I have seen the figures. I forget exactly what they are but the cost of the helicopters could be cut considerably. If something like that was brought in the government would certainly get the support of this caucus and of this member.

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to speak briefly on the responsible and far-sighted budget tabled this past Monday by the hon. Minister of Finance. Regardless of what those on the opposition benches say or would have the Canadian people believe, this budget aims to build on efforts outlined in the 1992 budget and the December 1992 economic statement. In the case of all three the objective is to position the Canadian economy for more growth in job creation by steadily reducing the burden of deficits and debt.
Since the budget was tabled many media critics have gone into high gear, producing a stream of so-called in-depth analyses of why the budget has failed the Canadian people. I figure this is fair game, for that is how the scribes earn their living.
However I find it galling to hear criticisms from the back benches of the Liberal Party. To me those in the Liberal caucus are unwittingly admitting that their memories are as lacking in substance as their alternative economic policies for dealing with Canada's fiscal problems.
To refresh those blocked memories let me say that it was the shortsighted, irresponsible policies of successive Liberal governments from 1968 to 1984 that provided fuel for the present fiscal crisis which threatens to bum away Canada's tomorrows.
Beyond a doubt it has not been an easy road for our government to travel in an effort to grapple with an inherited deficit that stood at more than $38 billion in 1984, the year we took office. Dealing with the problem has been far more difficult and complex than any of us could have imagined.
Many Canadians have not been particularly receptive to the brand of medicine we have been prescribing since 1984. However we have persevered and taken the slings and arrows of adverse public opinion in stride.

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
I believe some comparisons or results speak well of our approach to date. For example, during the recession of 1981-82 under a Liberal government the national debt increased by a phenomenal 160 per cent. During the recession we are now coming out of, the debt increased by only 19 per cent under our government.
In 1984 the deficit was 8 per cent of our Gross Domestic Product. Today the deficit has been cut to 4 per cent of the GDP. The increase in the national debt presently is not because of unbridled spending but rather the result of a significant decrease in federal revenues due to the recession.
When the election is called later this year and the people of Canada have the opportunity to really consider our medicine and compare it to the voodoo remedies of the opposition, I am confident they will make the right choice.
Let us face facts. There is no magic elixir. The debt crisis did not happen overnight and it most certainly will not be solved overnight. The reality of the situation is that there is no quick fix and there is certainly no magician who can wave a wand and proclaim, presto the debt is gone.
Although I admit the budget was not warmly received initially by the international economic community, the budget lays a solid base for a Canadian solution to a Canadian problem. Some of the high priced experts criticizing the budget were advocating an increase of 2 per cent in the GST and raising other federal taxes.
Yes, Canadians want to see an end to the deficit but they want to see it achieved through spending cuts and not higher taxes. We acceded to the wishes of the Canadian people and there are no new taxes or tax increases in this budget.
The budget cuts more than $30 billion from federal spending over the next five years. It builds upon the restraint measures introduced in the December 1992 economic statement. These measures will yield savings of $3.8 billion in 1993-94, rising to $7.9 billion in 1997-98 for a total savings of $30.7 billion.
These measures will also see the number of jobs in the federal Public Service reduced by 16,500 over five years. With further cuts in the federal departmental operating
budgets, together with the December economic statement wage freeze, the total savings over five years in this area alone will be $7.5 billion. By holding defence spending to zero real growth starting in 1994-95 combined with the 1992 restraint measures there will be a total savings of $5.9 billion over the next five years.
These measures are only the tip of the iceberg as far as the significant savings this budget will see accumulated over the next five years. This budget will see the deficit reduced to $32 billion this year, which is the target set out in December despite lower than expected revenues. It also aims to end new borrowing and begins the process of reducing publicly-held debt over five years.
Drastic cuts in spending are not the only budget measures. Building on the streamlining actions contained in the 1992 budget, 12 federal organizations will be eliminated, merged or restructured. For example the taxation and customs and excise departments will be amalgamated. In addition our government will be pursuing the privatization and commercialisation of a number of federal organizations and services to reduce the over-all size of government while improving the delivery of services.
There are areas left untouched by the budget. Although this is a tough budget it is also a fair one. Two major areas of public policy are exempt from the budgetary measures. Benefits for the elderly and veterans are again excluded from spending cuts. So are programs specifically geared to the disabled, certain native programs, the Canadian Jobs Strategy and famine relief.
In recognition of Canada's common fiscal problems, no additional restraint is being imposed on major federal transfers to the provinces. These will grow by almost 4 per cent a year, more than twice the rate of other federal program spending.
While we are speaking of the provinces, if it has not been abundantly clear in the past it certainly is now that the deficit and the debt are not the federal government's problems alone. All governments share responsibility for their creation and an equal responsibility for their reduction and eventual elimination. Frankly, the taxpayers of Canada want all governments to work together to find solutions to the national debt problem. That is why I
April 30, 1993

Government Orders
believe the most important aspect of the budget was the invitation extended by the Minister of Finance to all provincial and territorial finance ministers to attend a special meeting on May 30 and May 31 in Ottawa to begin the process of developing practical, co-operative solutions to our common fiscal problems.
I believe the planned meeting at the end of May is a significant step in the right direction. The federal government can slash spending from now until the cows come home, but unless all legislative jurisdictions in Canada pull together this problem will not be solved. Something concrete must be done to reduce the debt so succeeding generations will not continue to have a mortgage hanging over their futures. I do not believe for one moment that anyone wants to leave behind such a dismal legacy.
In conclusion, there are many who believe our government did not go far enough with the measures outlined in the budget. I disagree. To my way of thinking the budget provides a realistic approach to Canada's current fiscal problems, although the approach is gradual rather than radical. I believe it is both sensible and responsible. Yes, we could have made immediate cuts instead of phasing them in over five years and we could have raised taxes. However, in light of the fact that our economy is still recovering from one of the deepest recessions in recent memory the medicine is strong enough to do the job without killing off the patient.
The bottom line is simple and clear. Governments do not create jobs or enhance economic performance; the private sector does. I believe that the budget builds on the 1992 budget and the December economic statement by realistically attacking the number one dampener of economic activity, the deficit. In the final analysis less borrowing, lower interest rates and lower taxes are the best possible ways to stimulate economic activity and job creation at this time.
The previous speaker mentioned that one of the all-important reasons for our present financial situation is the proposed acquisition of the new helicopter program, the EH-101. I am aware that a great many in the opposition are giving the impression, probably not saying it so specifically, that the Government of Canada will be writing a cheque this year for $4.8 billion for the helicopter program. I happen to be a member of the Standing Committee on National Defence.
We had a very interesting and important meeting yesterday with the senior officials, the deputy minister and Admiral John Anderson, the chief of staff. I had the opportunity to question officials about this and of course listen to questions from my colleagues on the opposite side. In my remarks I stated that where we fell down badly was in getting the message across to the Canadian people. Even one of my distinguished colleagues on the Liberal side agreed with that.
The EH-101 program will do a job that is necessary. Sure there are no submarines lurking in our waters at the present time. I believe there are about 800 submarines owned by all the countries in the world. We know they are not a danger at the present time. It has not been emphasized enough that the EH-101 is a much superior aircraft and one of its most important jobs will be search and rescue.
It was mentioned in news reports that the new frigates coming on stream are not built to take the new EH-101-there are three frigates in the water now and there will be 12 within a very few years-and this was denied in no uncertain terms. They are built for that. The chief of staff and one of the other officials did mention that three of the Tribal class destroyers were not built to accommodate these new helicopters. There will be modifications made on those three quite old destroyers.
There was quite an article in the Times Colonist paper of Thursday, April 22. This is some information I would like to read into the record:
The mythical-cum-political version appears to have the following qualifications. Its selection was kept secret and was not debated until after the decision to buy it last summer.
It is an attack helicopter. Its sole purpose is to combat a non-existent cold war Soviet submarine threat.
Its other capabilities are far beyond our needs. It is the world's most expensive helicopter and costs $80-$ 90 million a copy. The project cost ballooned from $4.4 billion total to $5.8 billion and is unaffordable.
Moreover, Canadians will receive no significant benefits from this expenditure.
Listen to this:
It is too large to operate from a ship or to be maintained on board. Its limited range and fierce downwash make it unsuitable for search and rescue.

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
I could go on and on and on. Yet in answer to those negative remarks let us look into this:
Its selection in 1987 was highly publicized. In November 1990 the all-party Commons standing committee on national defence called the EH-101 the only contender for the Sea King replacement and recommended the replacement be done as soon as possible to avoid costly stopgap measures. It is a multi-role helicopter with three variants: naval, commercial heliliner and tactical/logistic transport.
The naval variant is designed for the surveillance and control operations against ships, submarines and aircraft and to provide early warning of anti-ship missiles or attacking aircraft. It also will enable its mother ship to conduct SAR, search and rescue, medical evacuation,evaluation, relief airlifts-
The EH-101 has the range, endurance, survivability and all-weather capabilities essential to cope with Canada's extremes of weather and large ocean areas of responsibility and to handle United Nations commitments in foreign seas.
Madam Speaker, I could go on but I just want to emphasize again that this new helicopter which will be purchased will be proven and will be accepted by the Canadian people. It is getting all the adverse publicity now because of a leadership convention which is taking place and also an election which may take place some time this year, if not a little later.

Madam Speaker, I would like to ask the hon. gentleman two questions. I have had the opportunity to sit on the environment committee with this gentleman for a couple of years and I respect him deeply.
I have a private member's bill C-301 which is an amendment to the financial act that is before the committee at the present time before it goes to third reading. I do not know if he is familiar with it but it is a bill on government accountability. I think it is a good bill and knowing the member and his common sense I was wondering if he could give me his views on that bill to help out on such situations as the budget.
My second question concerns the EH-101 helicopter. A close friend of mine in the city of Chatham is a helicopter pilot and owner who was with the United States Air Force and also flew for Jacques Cousteau in South America. He stated just Tuesday evening that the
Sea King can be refitted electronically to do everything the EH-101 will do. He explained that the EH-101 is only 20 miles an hour faster than the Sea King or the Bell helicopter. He said when you have a rocket coming at you at 700 miles an hour, 20 miles an hour means very little. It is the electronic system that is the important part of a helicopter. The frame can be replaced, the motor can be replaced, but the electronics is the most important part of a helicopter.
Now, we are getting 27 per cent of the work on this helicopter in Canada. Could we not get 100 per cent work in Canada by refitting our Sea Kings electronically?
I wonder if the hon. member would give his views on refitting our present helicopters as the United States has already done with theirs.

With respect to that private member's bill, I must admit I am not familiar with it. But let me tell you that I am in favour of anything that is going to make the government more accountable and I will say amen to that. speechtext: Don't worry about him Stan, he doesn't matter a bit.

speechtext:
Well all right. In any event, I am aware that there has been retrofitting of these helicopters in the United States. However the aircraft that are being refitted in the United States are much younger than
April 30, 1993

ours. Therefore, if we spend this money there is still a deadline of seven or eight years, and it would be an expenditure of $2.5 billion.
I think my colleague will agree that the majority of the Canadian people are against it. They are of the opinion that it may be the Minister of Supply and Services who will be writing the cheques and that the cheques will be written for $4.8 billion this year.
As I mentioned earlier in my remarks, when Admiral Anderson and his officials were before the Standing Committee on National Defence I brought up that very question. He pointed out to me that the EH-101 program this year will require a total expenditure of $200 million, rising gradually to a maximum of $700 million a few years from now and then reducing after that. In other words, there will not be a great savings this year whether the program is discontinued or not. Two hundred million dollars is not too much and that is what the program is costing Canadian taxpayers this year.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate on Bill C-117 to authorize the government to borrow the huge amount of $31 billion.
The previous speaker mentioned the helicopters. Without getting into the specifics of this project, it should be noted that we are buying a Cadillac and at this rate we will not even be able to afford to put gas in it. That is where we are at. I think we should reconsider this deal.
The deal was approved in 1990 and my hon. colleague referred to the unanimous report from the Standing Committee on National Defence. But the global situation has changed considerably since then and I do not think we need helicopters powerful enough to chase nuclear submarines which are no longer in service, seeing that the nations whose nuclear submarines were threatening us no longer exist as such. So, we should reconsider this whole thing.
Moreover, with respect to the helicopters, when you talk about 45,000 jobs being created, all that is based on getting contracts from foreign countries. But we know that the economy is in a critical state not only in Canada but world-wide. The chances of getting foreign contracts are minimal. So, why take such a risk? Instead of
investing $5.8 billion in a project which ultimately will not create that many jobs- actually few jobs will be created-the cost of this project is so high that we should really reconsider.
I notice that it is eleven o'clock, Madam Speaker. With your permission, I would like to conclude my comments on this bill after question period.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Very well. We will now proceed to Statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 31.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, last Thursday evening, I had the honour and the privilege to highlight the exceptional work done by 43 volunteers in my riding at a ceremony where they received the commemorative medal of the 125th anniversary of the Canadian Confederation.
The riding of Quebec-Est is packed with exceptional people and it was very difficult indeed to make a choice.
I want to pay a special tribute to these people who have contributed to improving the well-being of the population while strengthening community spirit.
I applaud these people who have given freely of their time, talen and energy for the education and cultural development of our society.

Madam Speaker, Monday's budget clearly proved that this government has no answer to the economic problems which have been with us for several years.
The deficit, unemployment, high and numerous taxes have hit Canadians hard, especially the middle class which pays more than its share of taxes in Canada.
They should have planned a complete overhaul of our tax system to ensure fairness for all Canadians without any special favours for the wealthy, as well as a national

April 30, 1993
technical training service so that our young people can take up their rightful place in our society.
Canadians are looking for a government with unshakable political will, to deal with the crisis we are now facing.

Madam Speaker, people in my riding want to see an end to the deficit. I recall the many times this was expressed to me over the past five years. They also want to see it achieved through spending cuts and not higher taxes. Although there are some who would like to see us spend more money on jobs, most agree that the government does not create jobs, the private sector does.
On behalf of my constituents in Wetaskiwin I ask all of our colleagues to commend the Minister of Finance for his persistent and consistent attack on the deficit. This budget cuts more than $30 billion over the next five years. It builds upon expenditure restraint measures introduced in the December 1992 economic statement. That will mean less borrowing, lower interest rates and lower taxes. My constituents agree that is the best way to stimulate economic activity and job creation.
I am particularly satisfied that the Minister of Finance has been able to begin national co-operation on all government debt. This is fundamental to ensuring continued economic recovery. We have to do it jointly with the provinces, and we encourage him and thank him for his continued efforts.

Madam Speaker, Monday's budget will do nothing to help bring about an economic recovery for the people of Cornwall. With unemployment at over 20 per cent and 37 per cent of the population relying upon some form of social assistance, Cornwall has received nothing from this budget to stimulate an economic recovery.
Since 1989 more than 20 factories and numerous businesses have ceased operations. In the last two and a half years 3,000 jobs have been lost through plant closures and lay-offs. This is the harsh reality of nine
years of Conservative government. This is its economic legacy.
With 1.5 million Canadians out of work, the economic mismanagement of the government has exacted an enormous human deficit which rivals the country's financial deficit. Fortunately Canadians will soon have an opportunity to put this government out of business. This will be one closure that will offer hope to the people of Cornwall for a brighter future.

Madam Speaker, the recent budget continues along the path of economic self-determination. Since my election the philosophy of this government has been to guide us gently back toward economic sanity after successive years of Liberal lavishness.
It would be heroic to be spenders. Spending more than the credit card allows, by the Liberals, robbed this past decade and maybe the next of this privilege.
Perhaps the best testimony for this budget has come from what we call an ordinary Canadian, my Ottawa landlady. A lifelong Liberal she concluded a discussion on the budget by pounding her fist on the kitchen table and saying it is a good budget. She said that we have the lowest interest rates in a lifetime and the lowest inflation in a lifetime. There are no new taxes, no tax increases and $30 billion in federal spending cuts.
The budget is everything we asked for. Compare that to what the now disappearing party has done to us. This is a good budget.

Madam Speaker, I had the opportunity to talk with a number of child care operators in my riding in Thompson, The Pas, and also with people from the Indian reserve in The Pas area.
They are very concerned about the fact that there is no national child care program. They are also concerned that the provincial government in Manitoba has cut the actual number of subsidized child care spots throughout the province. That means that women, quite often single parents, who need child care in order to take training to get off welfare and better themselves are not able to do so.
April 30, 1993

This government promised a child care program in 1984 and in 1988, but it is not following through. If we do not have a national child care program we only encourage more and more people to stay on welfare. That only increases the national deficit.
It is time for a national child care program to help those people who want to better themselves.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Supply and Services
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my opinion, Canadians should applaud this government's efforts to attract investment that generates jobs, whether we are talking about the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement or the North American free trade agreement.
A convincing example of what can be achieved was the announcement on March 1 this year that $160 million will be invested by a Spanish company, Petresa, in a petrochemical plant in Becancour.
The plant will produce additives for biodegradable detergents that will be sold throughout North America. Five hundred workers will be involved in construction of the plant, while another 75 will be employed in the plant on a permanent basis. The plant will make Canada a net exporter of this type of "green" product.
According to the president of the Spanish company, now that the North American free trade agreement was signed, the location on the St. Lawrence in Quebec will be ideal for shipping their products in Canada and to the United States and Mexico. Now that is free trade!

Madam Speaker, section 35(1) of the Fisheries Act states:
No person shall carry on any work or undertaking that results in the
harmful alteration, disruption or destruction of fish habitat.
Section 35(2) allows a person to contravene this subsection.
I call on the minister of fisheries to put a hold on the leases given in the Annapolis Basin by the provincial minister of fisheries in light of the people in the area having so many questions. The municipality of Annapolis wants to see the scientific studies before aquaculture begins. More important, the traditional fishermen want to see and question the studies. They want to meet with the elusive provincial minister of fisheries to ask him why he allowed aquaculture in an area so highly utilized when there are so many other areas around the coast.
There are many unanswered questions. I call on the federal minister of fisheries to make public the studies that were made in order for him to go against subsection (1) of section 35.

Madam Speaker, I would today like to call upon all members of this House, as well as all Canadians, to consider becoming an organ donor.
In Canada there are approximately 1,700 people waiting for an organ transplant at any one time. For some of these people a transplant will not come in time and they will die while waiting. Everyone has the potential to become an organ and tissue donor. The health of the donor, not the age, is the most important thing to consider.
Signing an organ donor card, whether separately or on the back of a driver's licence, is one way of indicating one's wishes to be an organ or tissue donor.
In closing, once again I ask all Canadians to consider becoming an organ or tissue donor. Let us all remember that if we are prepared to receive we must be prepared to give.

Madam Speaker, two weeks ago, Paul Watson, who is the

April 30, 1993
head of the Sea Shepherd Conservation Society, claimed his group had already spiked 20,000 trees in the Clayo-quot Sound region of B.C. and intend to spike a lot more. As well, he said he intends to teach a course in tree spiking in Tofino, which is in that region, at the end of this month.
Hidden spikes hit by saws send shrapnel flying indiscriminately and can tear through metal roofs and bodies like a machine gun. Mainstream environmental groups, the forest industry and the provincial government have all condemned Watson's statement. These threats are serious. As of November 27 of last year more than 40 spiked trees were found in one site of the disputed area. As of this time only the province of B.C. has legislation specifically outlawing tree spiking.
It is reported that the federal justice department has been preparing related amendments to the Criminal Code and I urge the government to immediately introduce such amendments, possibly in line with my own Motion M-767. My message to the government is: Nail the spikers now and incarcerate those who deliberately threaten the lives of loggers and woodworkers.

Madam Speaker, the 1993 budget is a mess. The Conservatives tell us that if they are re-elected they will add over $100 billion dollars to the debt. They also tell us that the deficit in the coming year will be $32.6 billion.
In reality the deficit would have been $33.25 billion but thanks to a shell game they managed to postpone $625 million in GST credit cheque refunds to low-income Canadians to next year's budget.
When the Tories talk about getting the country's finances back in order after nine years in government they really mean they are going to worsen the situation. When they talk about jobs they mean lay-offs.
What we need to get us out of this economic mess is a Liberal government that would not only look at the
balance sheet but also give its attention to stimulating the economy and job creation.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise today in support of the representations made by the Frontier Duty Free Association to the Ministers of Finance and National Revenue.
On behalf of the land border duty free shops, the association has sought an exemption from any possible potential reinstatement of the export tax on cigarettes.
Members of this House will know that no study has linked the sales by duty free shops to the tobacco smuggling problem. Departmental officials also have publicly acknowledged that these shops are not part of the problem.
In addition, to remove any doubt the duty free shops have worked co-operatively with our federal officials to ensure that they do not contribute to the tobacco smuggling problem.
Make no mistake about it. I continue to fully support our efforts to combat the problem of tobacco smuggling. However I would insist that the rather unique situation of these land border duty free shops, which employ over 700 Canadians, be given appropriate consideration.

Madam Speaker, I would like to publicly deplore the actions of an extremist right wing organization, the Heritage Front, along with others that are spreading hate propaganda, anti-Semitism and white supremacy in our community. The people of this city do not support this type of action.
We must protect the cultural mosaic of Canada. Our community requires a proactive approach. I am calling on the government to amend the Criminal Code to ensure effective means are implemented to deter hate propaganda.
Furthermore, I am calling on the government to facilitate the establishment of a working group in order to examine ways to ensure that racist organizations do not continue to flourish in our community.
April 30, 1993

Madam Speaker, the commanding officer of the Canadian Forces Marine Testing Range at Nanoose, B.C. recently announced that Canadian and U.S. Armed Forces have jointly committed to extending the agreement on the base for another 10 years. This fait accompli comes despite the fact that the base agreement does not even come up for renewal until 1996.
The base receives regular visits from nuclear powered and nuclear capable vessels. Documented accidents, including the disintegration of a Soviet nuclear submarine in Norwegian waters last fall, attest to the health and environment risks posed by these vessels.
There have been repeated calls for environmental impact studies to assess the dangers and for conversion of the base. A year ago the B.C. government declared the province a nuclear weapon free zone and earlier this month the city of Nanaimo voted to support conversion of the base to peacetime use.
The cold war is over yet the Canadian military has apparently entered into an agreement to continue cold war operations into the next centuiy.
When is the minister of defence going to take command of the Canadian Armed Forces and follow Canadian priorities rather than-

speechtext: I am sorry but the hon. member's time is up.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this year the federal government is highlighting the importance of consumer credit during National Consumer Week in order that consumers can act with full knowledge when they use the credit options that are available to them.
It seems clear that marketplace conditions affecting the use of credit have undergone fundamental changes and that these conditions are likely to persist.
Oral Questions
For example, while some types of consumer debts have declined from their recent peak level the use of consumer credit is still more common than it was a decade ago. Another change involves the misuse of credit, particularly credit cards.
To address this the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is communicating his concerns to the provinces and to credit grantors and asking them to provide their ideas on how problems of excessive indebtedness can be prevented and how the importance of the wise use of credit can be communicated effectively to consumers.
In addition to co-operative action with provincial governments and credit grantors, the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs will continue to make information on the wise use of credit available. This will help consumers better understand how to manage their credit responsibilities.

Madam Speaker, perhaps there is a minister who could answer a question on transport today.
Yesterday Hollis Harris, president of Air Canada, announced that there were more job losses in the works at Air Canada. The deterioration of the airline industry in Canada is a symbol of the government's incompetence.
On the one hand, the Minister of National Defence does not believe there is enough traffic in the industry for two airline companies, as she stated recently on the program aujourd'hui dimanche. On the other hand, the Minister of Transport has said, and I quote: "It is in the best interests of consumers and the travelling public to have two airline companies".
What is the government's policy on the future of the airline industry in Canada? Does the government have any idea what it wants for the future of that important industry?

April 30, 1993
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, it must be Friday. We get this question every Friday and the answer remains the same whether the Minister of Transport replies or I reply.
The answer simply is of course that the government is very concerned about the state of the airline industry as we are about the state of the airline industry around the world. Obviously in a recession and as a result of the gulf war airline industries around the world are in a difficult situation.
We are awaiting results of the NTA review of the current application of Canadian for an arrangement with American airlines. The government has got itself out of the airline business. We are waiting for a private sector solution. We are encouraged that one will soon be found.

Madam Speaker, I do not think the parliamentary secretary heard the drift of the question which raised new information that has come out recently.
He knows very well that in light of the decision of the competition tribunal last week, Canadian Airlines International is struggling to survive by seeking the co-operation of its employees and, most important, its creditors.
In the midst of all this the Minister of National Defence, a senior minister in government, decides to announce her learned opinion that Canada does not have enough traffic for two airlines. What message is she seeking to send to the creditors of Canadian Airlines? Is it that it is time to smash and grab? What message does the government have for those creditors?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as I said in my initial response, the position of the government has not changed in this regard at all.

The position has not changed. It does not have one, Madam Speaker.

As I said before, Air Canada president Hollis Harris announced yesterday there would be another substantial loss of jobs at Air Canada. Meanwhile, the government is
not charging Air Canada's competitors full landing fees and other taxes payable to the Government of Canada.
Why does the government maintain this double standard for air carriers? Why is the government just waiting for our airlines to go under?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of TVansport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think everyone in the House is aware of the difficult situation of Canadian Airlines and of all airlines in Canada at the present time. This kind of rhetoric does not help the situation at all.
We have been working very closely with all airlines in the country to ensure an ongoing competitive airline situation in Canada. The hon. member knows very well about our efforts, and again I do not think this kind of rhetoric helps the situation at all.

Madam Speaker, my question is not directed to the parliamentary secretary because his answers are entirely unsatisfactory. Air Canada has just announced that 2,200 employees will lose their jobs. This is not rhetoric. This is grim reality. We can blame the Conservative government for failing to act in the transportation sector.
I therefore want to ask one of the ministers from Quebec-not many are here today, but I would like to ask one of them-what this government intends to do to help Air Canada deal with its current economic problems, a company that under the Liberals was one of the seven best companies in the world and provided 24,000 jobs. I may remind the minister that today, Air Canada has only 6,000 employees in Montreal.
When will the Conservative government wake up and help this company remain viable, a Canadian company that creates jobs and keeps jobs in Montreal?

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of TVansport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I think I should respond by first mentioning that the Minister of Transport is a Quebec minister. The minister is very aware of the situation with regard to Air Canada.
April 30, 1993

However I go back to my response to the member for Ottawa South. World airlines are in a difficult situation as a result of (a) the gulf war and (b) the world recession.
This is not a situation unique to Canada. There is clearly overcapacity in Canada and these matters are being worked out.

Madam Speaker, the parliamentary secretary says this is a global problem. We are not talking about problems caused by the gulf war but about Tory policies, including deregulation, which created this problem facing Canadian companies today.
Earlier, my colleague asked some specific questions about Canadian airlines. I am now asking specific questions about Air Canada, and the parliamentary secretary tells us that the minister is from Montreal and he is keeping a close watch on the situation. The present minister may be from Montreal, but four of his predecessors were also from Quebec or the Montreal region and nobody has done anything whatsoever to help Air Canada.
Again, I want to ask when this government is going to get a consistent policy for the air transportation sector in order to save Canada's air transportation industry.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Richardson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, again I can appreciate the member's concern, coming late into this discussion.
On the other hand we have recently received the NTA report. One of the recommendations of the NTA report is on deregulation and how in fact it is working and working well across the country.

Madam Speaker, I share the concern of the hon. member of the Official Opposition who just spoke, but I would remind him the Liberals were the first to worship at the idol of
Oral Questions
deregulation under the Liberal Minister of Transport prior to their defeat in 1984.
My question is for the Minister of State for Finance and it has to do with the budget. It concerns the contrast between the rhetoric of the budget with respect to deficit reduction and the fact that no effort was made to close tax loopholes that had been identified previous to the budget and had been discussed in this House.
At least on one occasion the Minister of Finance indicated to me that he might have been considering reducing or eliminating the business and entertainment tax deduction that costs Canadians $1 billion a year. Could the minister say why no step was taken to address that particular tax measure?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, is that a question written by the hon. member from Windsor or is it one from the hon. member from Saskatchewan?
I will answer the question this way directly. The hon. member knows full well, because I saw him wining and dining with the Canadian Restaurant Association at the Chateau Laurier Hotel, that the Canadian Restaurant Association and the Canadian Small Business Association rely on those deductions for business purposes to help them with tourism, the restaurant business and small business.
New Democratic Party members stand and say that they are the great champions of small businesses but they certainly are not supporting them on this particular issue.

Madam Speaker, I do not know what the minister was consuming at that event but I certainly was not present.
In any event, the minister has given an argument in defence of that particular deduction, but the argument the Minister of Finance has given me in the past has had to do with staying competitive with the United States of America. This is the first time we have heard this particular angle.
Why was no effort made to close some of the tax loopholes that were identified by the Auditor General in his report? Surely, if deficit reduction is important, these

April 30, 1993
Oral Questions
kinds of loopholes should be addressed, particularly the ones which have been identified by the Auditor General. Why was no action taken on those particular loopholes?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I am not sure exactly what the hon. member is referring to when he talks about the Auditor General and loopholes.
Recently the Auditor General came out with a report saying that foreign companies were given an unfair advantage, but once the figures were compared with the Department of Finance and the situation examined there was a meeting of minds that maybe that was not entirely accurate.
I am not sure to what the hon. member is referring specifically. Let me say this. This government over the last nine years, the Government of Canada, has reduced or eliminated more tax loopholes, as they are commonly referred to, than any previous government.
The hon. member knows that. We have brought in minimum corporation taxes, large business taxes. We have brought in minimum taxes for banks and financial institutions. The hon. member knows we have gone a very long way. For him to stand here today and talk about tax loopholes and so on is really misleading the House.

Madam Speaker, I would agree that there were many tax loopholes to close, thanks to previous Liberal governments, but there are many tax loopholes yet to be closed by this particular Conservative government. Many of them have been identified over the last few years, and particularly over the last little while.
In a budget that was allegedly devoted to deficit reduction we saw absolutely none of these tax loopholes closed. I think it gives the lie to what the government is really up to.
Therefore could the minister explain, again with respect to tax loopholes, why the government refused to have anything to do with the proposed draft of the multilateral mutual assistance agreement by the 28 members of the OECD and the Council of Europe, a draft designed to take on the world's largest tax loopholes, preventing both evasion and avoidance of all taxes other than customs duties?
This treaty, more commonly known as Interfirpol, equips national governments to effectively deal with the formidable obstacles that global companies are constantly throwing at our national economies and at our national fiscal systems.
Why is it that the Canadian government has refused to try to create an international context in which one country cannot be played off against the other and on which ministers of finance do not have to constantly rise in this House and say they cannot close particular tax loopholes because it would make them uncompetitive?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find it interesting that the New Democratic Party and its spokesman today talk about the finance ministers from the IMF, the OECD and the G-7 playing off against one another, when it is just exactly the opposite.
The G-7 finance ministers are in the process of meeting in Washington before the IMF and World Bank meetings this weekend. I thought my hon. friend might be prepared to use some of the quotes such as that of Michel Camdessus, the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, who said: "My impression is that there is a very significant effort to take care of the public debt in Canada. The last developments are positive including the budget which was announced two or three days ago".
Answer the question.
Co-operation between countries and between finance ministers is ongoing. Thank goodness the NDP is not in there. There would be no co-operation at all.
What about the question I asked?

Madam Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
The minister of defence claims she did not know that the beating death in Somalia on March 16 involved criminal intent until March 31. Yet statements by the chief of defence staff show clearly that she knew on March 19.
Yesterday the Minister of National Defence called the statement of the chief of defence staff ridiculous.
April 30, 1993

My question for the Acting Prime Minister is this: Does he agree with the Minister of National Defence or does he, as we do, believe the chief of the defence staff? If he does, would he agree to open up the Somali inquiry to include a thorough examination of the role of the minister?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
To begin with the hon. member has not represented the situation factually in terms of what actually was said by either the Minister of National Defence or the chief of the defence staff.
The chief of the defence staff in his briefing indicated that the unit reported evidence indicating that criminal intent might be linked. He indicated that it might be linked. The hon. member said that the Minister of National Defence therefore knew there was criminal intent. She knew no such thing, nor did the chief of the defence staff say so. He said there might be.
What happens when there is an indication that there might be? An investigation is appointed and it is investigated by the appropriate authorities. That is precisely what the Minister of National Defence indicated was happening. It was being investigated. It is up to the investigation to make that determination.
The hon. member knows, if he attended the briefing of the Judge Advocate General, that the Minister of National Defence has a role in the defence legal system not dissimilar to that of a judge. If in fact the Minister of National Defence had stated explicitly on the 7th: "Yes, criminal intent," the hon. member quite rightly could have stood in this House demanding her resignation immediately for acting irresponsibly.
She said all she could say. She did not misrepresent the situation, nor in fact is there any conflict between what she said and what the chief of the defence staff said.

Madam Speaker, there clearly is a conflict. If the minister is in fact correct then she has nothing to hide from a public inquiry then surely a public inquiry would exonerate her.
Oral Questions
If, as Canadians believe and we believe, there is a contradiction between what the chief of the defence staff said and what the minister said, they cannot both be right. In order to arrive at the truth why does the government not open up the inquiry to include a thorough examination of the role of the minister? If she is right she has nothing to hide.

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State and Leader of the Government in the House of Commons):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
To begin with, what particular accusation is the hon. member making in terms of the Minister of National Defence? Is he suggesting that as Minister of National Defence she should have come out and stated explicitly all the details?
Let me repeat my first answer because obviously he did not hear it: Indicating criminal intent might. Indicating might. Think about those two words, "indicating might". That was concluded.
She did not say that.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Now the hon. member is shouting at me and will not listen to my answer even though he asked the question. Supposedly he treats this issue seriously. If he did he would close his jaw and listen to my answer.
The reality is that the inquiry was set up to establish the truth in respect of the operations of the Canadian Armed Forces units in their peacekeeping role. They are not dealing with a criminal investigation which is gomg on by the appropriate authorities under the jurisdiction of the Judge Advocate General.
The reality is in order that there be full and frank discussion by the witnesses it is being held in camera. The hon. member is suggesting that unless it is being held under the full light of TV cameras and so on we will not know the truth. Therefore, he s suggesting that the commissioners on this commission cannot be trusted to establish the truth. I would like him to name the commissioners he thinks are untrustworthy.

My question is for the Acting Prime Minister. Today is tax day for Canadians. Since it was elected this government has spent $1 trillion of their money. That is a one followed by 12 zeros. The deficit has grown to $34 billion. The debt is

April 30, 1993
Oral Questions
approaching $500 billion. We have been through a three-year recession and 1.5 million Canadians are out of work.
As Canadians write their cheques to the government they want to know this: Just what is going on here? What does this government think it is doing to this country?

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
I hope I have the time to answer this.
First of all, some very good news came out this morning. The real gross domestic product rose four-tenths of 1 per cent in February. Over the last three months real domestic product growth has grown at an average annual rate of 4 per cent. I might point out that goods production increased 5 per cent. All those are good signs. Those are signs that the economy is coming back.
rhis government has placed Canada in a position to take advantage of recovery. We have the lowest interest rates in 30 years, lowest mortgage rates in 30 years and the lowest inflation rate in probably 20 years. As late as yesterday we were being credited by the IMF, by the treasury secretary of the United States and others that Canada is going to have the best job growth and the best gross domestic product growth over the next two years.
That speaks well for the very tough decisions this government, the finance minister and the Prime Minister have had to take over the last few years to bring us to this point. We said this is what would happen. It is happening and we are very pleased to see it.

Madam Speaker, when we have hit the depths this government has taken us to there is no place to go but up, is there?
If the minister wants opinions on the budget I will give him opinions on it: "From a tired government a budget without inspiration; a bloodless budget; a phoney budget; and more razzmatazz".
This government that promised Canadians no tax increases has given them 38 new taxes or tax increases. What does this budget promise them? It promises them more tax increases. For the next five years personal income taxes will increase by over 7 per cent. That is 36
per cent in this budget. Just what is this government doing with their money? Canadians want to know why they should trust it with one more cent.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Finance and Privatization)):
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I find that passing strange. We were criticized by the business community and some of the financial thinkers in this country for not raising taxes. Now my hon. friend is coming out and saying that we are raising taxes. The first statement by the Minister of Finance in the budget was that there were no new taxes and no increase in taxes. We are standing by that because we think that will help recovery.

Madam Speaker, I have the pleasure of submitting the following bill for first reading, entitled an act to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act.
The purpose of this bill is to amend the Public Service Superannuation Act in order to address the plight of federal public servants who lost their jobs since 1988 due to downsizing.
Currently a public servant who has reached the age of 55 and has at least 10 years of service and chooses a pension because he or she is a victim of downsizing is entitled to a full pension. However the same is not true for public servants between the ages of 50 years and 54 years. If pensioned they are penalized by 5 per cent a year until age 60 which means a 50 per cent reduction of their already minuscule pension. My bill would correct the situation by decreasing the 5 per cent a year reduction from age 60 to age 55. These public servants, many of whom cannot find employment, would then be able to receive 75 per cent of their minuscule pension instead of the present 50 per cent in face of the 1993 budget which calls for a further 16,500 public servant positions to be cut.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
With respect to the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency the government has taken the following action to resolve the problems outlined in the 1991 Auditor General's report:
(a)	Appropriation of funds
The primary concern of the office of the Auditor General (OAG) was that the agency was advancing funds before commercial production was achieved. In this regard, the agency reviewed the policies relating to commercial production. It was found that the definition of the date of the commencement of commercial production requires 30 continuous days of production of marketable goods in commercial volume. This left no room for discretion and caused difficulties for seasonal operators and some small entrepreneurs. All references to this milestone date have been removed from the terms and conditions, but retained in the guidelines where the agency has sufficient authority to reasonably deal with problem situations. This amendment to the terms and
April 30, 1993

conditions of the action program was approved by Treasury Board on April 30, 1992 (TB 818236).
(b)	Treatment of documents
The concern of the OAG related to two points:
1.	Treatment of sector department advice.
The agency has reaffirmed the need for ACOA officers to document all correspondence with sector departments and to ensure that all concerns are addressed and resolved before further processing of an application. Verification of adherence to this procedure will be established as part of the quality assurance audit regime.
2.	Treatment of substantive amendments
The agency's practice has been to define as substantive amendents those which increase the financial exposure of the federal government or could adversely affect the commercial viability of the project.
Using these criteria as a guide, a review of substantive and non-substantive amendments, as defined in section 400-1 delegation of authorities, policy and procedures manual, was conducted.
After careful consideration it has been determined that the listing of substantive amendments is appropriate and that no changes are warranted.
It is agreed that in the case identified by the OAG, the amendments to the project should have been considered as significant and therefore should have been approved by the minister. This is a case where the procedures were not applied properly and not a case where a policy change is warranted.
(c)	Evaluations of projects prior to their approval
The primary concern of the OAG was that the agency did not conduct adequate evaluation of commercial viability before the project was approved.
In this regard the agency has initiated two steps:
1.	The agency is in the process of implementing an automated financial analysis package. Financial and other indicators directly assessing the commercial viability of a project are an inherent part of this package. This will ensure quality and consistency in the evaluation of the applicant's financial situation.
2.	A comprehensive training package for account managers has been designed and will be applied to 70
Routine Proceedings
ACOA officers before fiscal year end. Among the topics covered will be the various evaluation criteria which have to be addressed before a project is approved.
(d)	Terms and conditions under which the agency was created
The terms and conditions of the action program are under constant internal review and challenge, to ensure they reflect the best practice of combining protection of the public purse while promoting regional development.
As part of this effort, the agency recently completed a full evaluation of the action program. This evaluation included a detailed review of the impacts and effects of the terms and conditions and offered recommendations for improvements. The agency will be announcing the results of the evaluation in the near future and subsequently formulating an action plan to deal with the recommendations.
Related actions
The agency has improved systems, processes, and policies to address the OAG findings. However, the coverage by the OAG indicated cases where, although policy and prescribed procedure is satisfactory, there was non-compliance with the terms and conditions of the action program. To minimize the potential of such cases, the agency has taken the following two measures:
-Project monitoring

The new tenant made a further assignment of its leasehold interest to Chambers Ottawa (1992) Inc., a corporation controlled by Perez Corporation and The Standard Life Assurance Company. As indicated in NCC chairman's letters to the hon. member for Carleton-Gloucester dated November 2, 1992 and December 2, 1992, Chambers Ottawa (1992) Inc. approached the National Capital Commission in November 1991 with a proposal to provide head office accommodation to the commission at the Chambers site. While the commission was considering issuing a proposal call for its head office accommodation in the national capital region, it agreed to review the proposal submitted by Chambers Ottawa (1992) Inc.
The commission's consideration of the proposal was compatible with its mandate, given its responsibility for safeguarding federally designated heritage buildings. The commission was concerned about the possible ramifications to the project from the stagnation of the commercial leasing market, both in terms of the risk of
delays and hence damage to the structures in question and the potential delay in receiving participation ground rent under the terms of the ground lease.
The Chambers site was found to be a desirable and justifiable head office location. However it became impossible to proceed by way of a public tender for the site's development due to the existing ground lease. After reviewing the proposal submitted and performing the necessary due diligence, the commission proceeded to enter into negotiations for a building lease with Chambers Ottawa (1992) Inc. on a sole source basis. The decision to proceed in this manner was taken only after a comparative analysis showed that the terms of the lease being proposed were competitive, given the heritage nature of the project and the terms of the ground lease in effect.
