subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, as I was saying before being interrupted at 11 a.m., I am pleased to participe in this debate on Bill C-117, an act to provide borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning on April 1, 1993.
The Conservative government is asking Canadians through Parliament for authorization to borrow over $31 billion in order to meet certain expenditures. The Conservative government is responsible for the management of public funds. It wants our trust and the power to borrow over $31 billion, which is an enormous amount of money. Given the sad economic performance of this government during the past decade and its empty budget of this week, we have no other alternative but to say no.
The government claims to be borrowing the amount indicated in Bill C-117 to complete public works and for general purposes. This could mean just about anything. This amount is also roughly equivalent to the anticipated deficit of $32.6 billion for the 1993-94 fiscal year, in last Monday's budget. You can rest assured that if the Conservative government could it would ask us for even more money later to fill the void created by a deficit which is even greater than expected.
That has already happened in the past, that the government comes back for additional borrowing. We know very well that all the budget predictions which this government made in eight and a half years, nearly nine years, and even those in the last budget never came true. Fortunately that party has only a few months left in
Government Orders
power, because in the next election the people will change the government.
I would like to take a closer look at the problem of the deficit and the debt. On May 23,1985 when he presented his first budget, the then Minister of Finance said that if he did not attack the debt problem the Government of Canada would end up paralyzed. At that time the public debt was a little under $200 billion. To solve the debt problem, the Conservative minister proposed tough measures needed to reduce the deficit and thus reduce the growth in the debt.
Let us look at the result of nine years of "tough measures", as the minister called them. The public debt has risen from $200 billion to over $450 billion in just nine years. In other words, the government's measures more than doubled the national debt; that is, the Conservatives are responsible for creating more debt in nine years than all the debt created in the previous 117 years of Canada's history.
The then Minister of Finance said in 1984 that if the debt problem was not dealt with Canada would be paralyzed. Well, the minister was right because today, thanks to his unsound economic policies, the country is in an unparalleled economic slump. Instead of solving the problem of the deficit and the debt, the Conservatives only made it worse. The figures are there and we could talk for hours, days and even months and go over all the budgets the two Conservative ministers presented since 1984.
The government's economic policies were as ineffective in dealing with the problem of high unemployment as they were with the deficit and the debt. In 1984 the Minister of Finance told this House that his policies were meant to "break the vicious circle of unemployment and public debt".
Let us now look at the problem of high unemployment and its harmful effects. Today, Canada has about 1.6 million jobless, and that is just the official figure. I say official because those who have given up looking for a job are not counted as unemployed by Statistics Canada.
The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops believes that there are now nearly four million unemployed people, welfare recipients and others without work in Canada. According to the Conference, the fact that a quarter of the country's labour force is thus excluded from the labour market undermines society's moral

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
fibre. The bishops blame the economic policies of the last decade for this situation. High unemployment costs us dearly, also in terms of actual dollars and lost production, which is hard to estimate.
Let us take an example. Canada's Unemployment Insurance Plan costs employees and employers about $18 billion. If the unemployment rate were cut in half with job creation programs, $9 billion would be saved. Can you imagine what could be done with such an amount? To these $9 billion add another $6 billion that could be obtained if the government had the courage to cancel the purchase of 50 EH-101 helicopters.
It is an insult to our intelligence when candidates for the leadership of the Conservative Party tell us that they are concerned about the deficit. To solve the problem they say that all spending is on the table, even the universality of our social programs. We must be clear when we talk about social programs. Only one of them is still universal: health insurance. These people talk about abolishing the universality of medicare, a program which is the envy of the whole world.
Instead, why not put the purchase of these helicopters on hold? They are ready to eliminate the universality of Medicare, but they are not willing to give up the helicopter program. It is like buying a Cadillac without having the money to put gas in it.
There would be no limit to the problems which could be solved with a simple readjustment of priorities. Unfortunately, the priorities of this government are totally absurd. This government overlooks the human side of the situation. The first priority of a government should be the people. It may well be that such a priority would help alleviate the suffering in this country. If you want to see people suffering, come to Montreal. The poverty level is simply tragic!
According to Statistics Canada, Montreal breaks every record in terms of poverty for a metropolitan area. Indeed, 22 per cent of Montrealers live below poverty level. Twenty tons of food are now distributed each day in Montreal. What is even sadder is the fact that street children in Montreal know the same fate as those in Rio, according to a report from the World Health Organization. And then yesterday evening we learned that Air Canada intends to lay off 2,200 employees, bringing the total to 7,000 since 1990.
Will the Minister of Transport, who is also responsible for the Montreal region, examine the effects of his laissez-faire policy in Montreal? It used to be said that Montreal was a city with pride. Today, we say that it is the capital of poverty. Such is the sad reality of the Montreal region.
In my area, namely the east end of Montreal, the unemployment rate exceeds 25 per cent. Do you wonder why we refuse to support the government's decision to borrow over $31 billion? Its priorities are totally off. The government did not unveil any job creation program in last Monday's budget. It continues to make helicopters a priority instead of people.
This government showed nothing but economic inertia over the last decade. It has failed miserably. That is why we will vote against Bill C-117. We will vote against this government's budget policy and the people of Canada will vote against this inhuman and incompetent party in the next election.
The budget tabled last Monday is a disgrace. It brings nothing new and, what is worse, the Minister of Finance has given in to the prospect of a jobless recovery. If a small business had handed the same kind of budget to its bank manager he would have cut its credit and rejected any loan application.
There is nothing in this budget. Worst of all, this creative bookkeeping has been going on for years. It started with source deductions. They increased the frequency of source deductions to twice a month so that they could show a lower deficit at the end of the fiscal year. They used the same system for the federal sales tax rebate.
I clearly recall that when questioned on its GST policy and its impact on the poor and the old, the government answered: "We have a program whereby we will send them a cheque every three months." This was meant to compensate them for an unfair regressive tax they would have to pay on consumer goods.
And now, the government announced in Monday's budget that they will no longer get four cheques a year but just two, starting in January 1994. Why not immediately? If these programs save as much money as the government claims, why not apply this measure to the next two payments? First, because with an election coming they are afraid that the people will speak their minds about this government and send it off to collect UI benefits. Also, the first payment will be due in January
April 30, 1993

1994, and the second would be due in April under the old quarterly payment system but its fiscal year ends March 31. So, what does this government do? It starts by eliminating one payment of the GST tax refund to the needy and uses an accounting trick. This way it can predict that by March 31, 1994 the deficit will have been reduced. There will be no real reduction because the same cheques for the same total amount will have to be sent out during the first week of April, but it will be a new fiscal year by then.
That is how this government has always got around the debt and deficit problem, by increasing our taxes. This needs to be said. A report published this week says that Canadians have seen their taxes increase by 25 per cent since this government took office. That is a 25 per cent tax increase. That is where we are at. That is the present situation. We had a projected annual deficit of about $32 or $33 billion, with a national debt of about $180 billion. But even with a 25 per cent increase in taxes the debt has now grown to more than $450 billion, while the deficit remained at the same level. That is what the Tories' economic policies have done.
I remember in 1983 when the present Minister of Trade who was finance critic at the time said that tax increases would completely stop economic growth. But this Finance Minister has increased taxes more than any other in the history of our country. This is where the Tories have led us after nine years in power.
One other thing. There is nothing in this budget for our young people. What does this government do for our youth? What hope does it give them to find a job after graduating? No jobs are created, thus there are none for young Canadians. Each time we bring up the issue of drop-outs we are told this is in provincial jurisdiction. Why would they pursue their education to be better equipped for the future when they see their brothers, sisters, cousins and neighbours make sacrifices to get an education but find no job when they graduate? That is the situation this government has created over the past nine years. It has doubled, almost tripled the debt. The deficit has remained unchanged. Taxes have been increased on 32 occasions. It has implemented the GST which not only slowed down the economy, but forced a
Government Orders
big part of it underground. That is why our young people are discouraged and the future is uncertain.
I have not spoken of the famous free trade deal yet. During the 1988 election campaign, we were told it would bring prosperity. Canada would be open to the whole world, which would bring prosperity to all Canadians. Today we see plants closing and companies moving south where they will continue to sell us their products, maintaining their sales while we are losing jobs in Canada.
Unfortunately, this government cannot be given carte blanche to go out and borrow $31 billion without some reckoning as any good manager would be called on to give. The forecasts the Minister of Finance provided us on Monday are neither realistic nor logical and they continue to lead the country in the wrong direction. Unless we change course, we will have the Cadillac of helicopters but no money to buy fuel to run them.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1993-94 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, Bill C-117 is an act to provide borrowing authority for the fiscal year beginning on April 1, 1993 and it deals with the Financial Administration Act.
Over the last few months we heard a lot about the deficit and the damage it spells for our economy.
I certainly do not want to trivialize the fact. Of course the deficit must be kept under control. Common sense tells us we cannot let the deficit get out of control. However, the way this government has been managing the deficit leaves much to be desired.
Some time ago, I was listening to CBC radio, and a professor of economics at Saint John's University in Manitoba was talking about the deficit. After hearing some very interesting comments by Professor Reuben Carl Bellan, I managed to get his home telephone number and we talked for about fifteen minutes about what he said on the radio. Later, I read an article in the paper.
Professor Bellan made it clear that the deficit must be properly managed. He argued that today Canada issues bonds to finance the deficit. It borrows money on the bond market. In recent years, many bonds were purchased by Germany, Japan, the United States, Sweden and other countries. I don't know the exact figures, but we are talking about billions of dollars coming in to be used to cover Canada's deficit.
According to Professor Bellan, that was a mistake, because in Japan, for instance, the government does not allow financing of domestic debt with foreign funds. Japan has an enormous deficit, but it is financed only by the Japanese. No American, Canadian or German funds are being used to finance Japan's deficit.
April 30, 1993

Professor Bellan argued as follows: Why does Canada allow non-Canadians to buy Government of Canada bonds? It should keep transactions in Government of Canada bonds in Canada, to be made by Canadians, because Canadians buy Canadian products and pay taxes in Canada. The Japanese, Germans, British or Americans who buy Government of Canada bonds do not pay taxes in Canada. Elis point was that when these funds come from outside the country, we have a real debt.
Let me explain. It would be fine if foreign funds were used to finance infrastructures or were invested in our industry, to make it more productive and more efficient. But that is not the case. This foreign money is largely used to finance our deficit.
Professor Bellan went on to talk about the time between 1939 and 1945, when we were at war. Obviously we had to defeat the Nazis. Canada had to mobilize vast numbers of people across the country. Considering Canada's population that was a formidable undertaking. In 1944 and early 1945 Canada's cumulative deficit was $18 billion. Not impressive, compared with today's figures. However, w'hen we consider the value of the current dollar, our gross domestic product and our ability to pay, $18 billion was just as bad as today's cumulative deficit of $460 billion. In fact, we were in worse shape as far as our ability to pay was concerned. In other words, at the time it was harder to pay back $18 billion than it is to pay back the federal government's $460 billion deficit today. How did we do it?
According to Professor Bellan, in 1944-45 economists were very pessimistic about the post-war period. Canada would be debt-ridden. We would all be dressed in rags and live in shacks. They painted a horrific picture. However, we went on to a period of unprecedented prosperity. Their predictions were all wrong. However, economists have always been better at explaining their own mistakes than predicting the future. We have to remember that.
Professor Bellan made another interesting point. From 1939 to 1945 when Canada's deficit was even worse in real terms than it is today, who financed the deficit? Canadians did. Obviously it was not the Germans who financed Canada's debt during the war in
Government Orders
1939-1945. Canadians financed the deficit by purchasing Victory Bonds.
I suppose we could ask this professor from Manitoba, and someone did: What if Canadians don't have enough money to finance the debt? Good question. We do have enough money. Today, Canadians have more than $300 billion in Canadian banks, ten times as much as this year's deficit.
Canadians have the money, and this government must start by financing its debt with money from within our money. When Canadian money is used to pay off the debt it does not have the same impact as when foreign money is used. I think this is just common sense and I think that perspective could be used for all our problems. It may be one of the alternatives we have today.
It is often said that the government creates jobs. Some people agree and others do not. I tend to disagree. Let me explain. Under our democratic system the government has the power to raise taxes and pass laws. Those are the two most important powers it has in a democratic society. It can raise taxes and adopt legislation through Parliament. If a government has these two fundamental instruments in a society like ours it does not have to intervene in any other sector.
Crown corporations may have been necessary in the past but I think they no longer are today. Personally I think the government's role and I know there are others who share my opinion, is to ensure that laws are just, that the tax system is fair and equitable-which is not the case here in Canada-and that programs and policies are sensible and necessary, which is not always the case either in Canada today.
We do not want any frills. We want the government to provide for programs that meet the needs of Canadians. Those programs are badly needed.
When we hear people say the government is going to create jobs we have every reason to be suspicious. However, the government can create a climate of confidence. It is absolutely necessary if we want Canadians to invest in their country. If we want to have foreign investment investors must be assured of a climate of confidence in Canada, that we have hope and are moving forward.

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
How can the government achieve this? It is very easy. It must ensure that the tax system is fair and equitable- this is basic, especially in a democratic society like ours. At the present time, it must be said that the middle class is paying more than its share. I have said that many times and I repeat it again. When will we admit in this House that the middle class pays more than its share and that this cannot continue? We need a thorough reform to change this state of affairs.
I just spoke about our accumulated deficit and I added that Canadians alone should pay for the deficit. When I look at what other countries do, I ask myself some questions. When I see that other countries can reform their tax system, like New Zealand, and when I see the tax rate on big multinationals in Germany and Japan, I wonder whether Canada could not do the same. Are we more stupid than they? Can we not find ways to assure all Canadians that we are making a very sincere attempt to correct this shortcoming, that other countries have been able to get back on track by making reforms and that they have gained others' confidence? I think that is basic and we must use common sense. That is all Canadians ask and that is what we must work on.
Let us talk about social programs now. Oh, I have read many times that our social programs are too costly; the big multinationals are always saying that. However, the figures show the contrary. I called the Auditor General, who sent representatives to my office because I wanted to study what has happened to the federal government's budget and deficit since 1972. Yes, social programs are important, but they did not contribute as much to the deficit as some would have us believe.
The accumulated deficit is $460 billion, but social programs account for barely 6 per cent of that. They are not what hurt our economy the most. Social programs as such are not responsible for the deficit.
I believe that I speak for the great majority of Canadians when I say that health insurance is one of the most important assets in our society. Medicare started in Saskatchewan and those responsible for this plan are to be congratulated.
Even for me, a citizen of Canada from Quebec, health insurance is one of the programs that I am the most proud of and it should never be attacked. It can be modified and user fees can be charged. We must not be afraid of change, but it must continue to provide all
Canadians with the medical care they need. This program is absolutely necessary and it must never be called into question.
Other social programs, like the old age pension, are a source of pride for our country. I wonder if many Canadians realize that the United States, the richest country in the world-or one of the richest, because we must not forget Japan and Germany-has no old age pension.
This shows that our priorities are different from the Americans'. We are not criticizing them, far from it, but when we look at what we have built together here in Canada, what is our basic philosophy? We are our brother's (and our sister's) keeper. That is healthy and right and good for our country. If my neighbour needs help or medical care, he is entitled to receive it. Is there anything more wonderful in our country than that? Is there anything more wonderful than an unemployed person being able to collect unemployment insurance, when you think about it? Yes, there is abuse, but that is human behaviour. We know that, you and I. Perhaps over time, with more civic mindedness, people will realize that social programs should never be abused. We may not be at that point yet but it is coming, I am convinced.
We hear a lot about the deficit as though it were a bogeyman. I do not want to trivialize the deficit; it is serious. But as I said, corrective action can be taken, funding to begin with, and perhaps also an analysis of present programs. Certainly some programs and policies are out of date and need to be changed. We must not be afraid of change; we need political will. A government with political will can work miracles, I am not exaggerating. But without this conviction and this political will nothing is possible. We waste our effort by finding all sorts of excuses and rationalizing the errors and disadvantages of the various options.
Unfortunately my time is nearly up, but in the few minutes available to me, I would like to talk about youth. All my colleagues in this House are aware that there is a deep unease among our youth. I am convinced that there are answers to it, and I did not invent them, far from it. What we need is a national training service. I am not talking about a military service at all; there is no military connotation. I am talking about a national training service in co-operation with the provinces. This kind of program has been very successful in Germany, a tremen-
April 30, 1993

dous success. I have documentation in my office and I have gone over it.
Here in Canada, occupational training may be one of the solutions for our youth. Personally, I know that if young people were given training for up to two years in a trade school and given technical knowledge we could greatly reduce youth unemployment and give young people hope. That is fundamental. Think of these young Canadians, be they 16, 26 or 27 years old, whatever, who are no longer in high school, who did not finish secondary school, who have no trade and no technical skill, who are on unemployment insurance or not working. You know as well as I do that they have no future. A national training service would be a solution for them.
At the present time more than 300,000 jobs in Canada are unfilled because these jobs need technical knowledge, basic knowledge of the industry or high technology. University diplomas are not at all required but rather technical schools, apprenticeships, trade schools that will help our young people overcome their difficulties.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I thank you for your patience. I repeat, there are solutions. Above all, it takes courage to face the real problems and then to have the political will to go ahead and make the required changes, whatever the cost. It is for the good of our country and of every province and community, for the good of our neighbours on the right and on the left and across the way.

Mr. Speaker, in addressing the borrowing authority matter before us there are a number of comments I want
Government Orders
to make concerning four specific areas of government activity or the lack of government activity. I want to preface those with a few general comments about the economic direction, or lack of it, which this government has imposed on Parliament and the people of Canada.
The government is very fond of referring to these times as recessionary times. It is my opinion and that of many others across Canada that this has not been a recession like the others. In fact it is open to some question as to whether the term recession has been appropriate at all.
What we have been experiencing for the last number of years, particularly since 1988, is more like a major structural implosion which has been exacerbated by the fall-out of the free trade agreement between Canada and the United States and some of its implications, and looking ahead to the psychology taking root because of the impending North American free trade agreement.
These and other actions have caused a major "restructuring" which has destroyed much of our manufacturing industry base, particularly in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario, but also in areas of the lower mainland of British Columbia, those areas that were in the lead in terms of a Canadian manufacturing industry and a resource-based processing industry.
To term that kind of basic restructuring, which has seen not just large-scale lay-offs but large-scale terminations and the creation of rust belts in Quebec and Ontario and other manufacturing and industrial areas, a recession is false. Many of those jobs will not come back.
We recognize that the world is changing and that the global marketplace has different dynamics than it had at one time. However those have been added to by the very kinds of actions that this government in Canada has taken.
Moving from that very general statement, when we look at the so-called economic planning of this government since it was first elected in 1984, and its constant hyping and high-frequency alarms about debt and deficits, some of them justified, that have been constantly forthcoming from the government, particularly from its finance ministers, what have we found?

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
The over-all debt picture of Canada has been getting worse and worse despite the efforts of this government. While it says with some braggadocio that the percentage of debt as related to the GDP is somehow better or our annual deficit positions are better its projections have constantly been way out. It has been deficit and debt reduction on the never-never plan.
We see almost exactly the same annual deficits now that we saw when this government was first elected in 1984, even with the rather profligate spending versus revenue generation policies of the Trudeau government that preceded it. It has been totally out of whack but it keeps saying things are looking up.
When one is flat on one's back even the bottom rung of the ladder looks high. That is about the only way that one can put any optimism into the economic scenario and the debt and deficit scenario that surrounds all of us, not only the federal government but those provincial governments who have been further encumbered by the cutbacks and the offloading that this federal government has participated in.
I am not going to suggest that it has done that with glee for it has certainly gone to great pains to disclaim its share of the responsibility for the difficulties that many provinces are having.
I would suggest that one of the irresponsible results of that action has been the drastic increase in our foreign debt, which is much more harmful to our long-term planning in this country than the domestic debt. The debts and deficits we had prior to this government taking office in 1984 were largely domestic.
Almost every economist would agree that we are in a much more serious situation as a result of a far higher percentage of our national and provincial debts being owed on the foreign market rather than within Canada's borders.
I said when I began that I specifically wanted to refer to four particular items that both my region and my industry, the forest industry, views with some alarm.
First of all, I want to go back to 1983 and then to 1984 and examine what at that point was the thrust of the former federal government and this federal government with regard to the forest industry, intensive silviculture
and paving the way for what we hoped would be a healthier and more dynamic forestry sector. After all it is the major contributor to our balance of payments situation on the plus side and has its roots in every part of Canada in some 300 communities.
I think Mr. Roberts was the minister in the Trudeau government in 1983 when we had the first federal-provincial agreement on funding of intensive forestry and silviculture between the forestry provinces and the federal government.
In the case of British Columbia that worked out to $55 million a year from the federal government, for that one year, and $55 million from the province of British Columbia. It was a good start but it was short term and the government changed.
It was one of the best things this government had done, even though on an annual basis there was a slightly smaller commitment. It dropped from $55 million a year to $50 million a year in the case of British Columbia.
With extensive negotiations they established three-year and five-year forestry agreements between the federal government and the provinces that allowed for some long-term planning and some good co-ordination. It was far more cost effective, there was far more bang for the buck, and it did far more for the forest industry across this country in restocking some of the areas that had been left lying dormant for far too long and beginning to use some of the new technologies in terms of intensive silviculture and practices such as thinning, pruning, fertilization, and many other areas that had long been missing from what had been one of our most vital industries. Starting in 1983 for the first time but especially after this government took office in 1984, we saw some rational planning and significant commitment to that sector in a way that counted. All of us with emotional and financial roots in that industry were very happy to see that take place.
.(1315)
My party and I certainly recognize that forestry falls essentially within provincial jurisdiction, but federal governments for decades have derived large revenues from that industry. Many of us, including the government, I suspect, but certainly the Minister of Forestry when that ministry was established during the years of this government felt that it was long past the time that

some of those revenues the federal government had been receiving for decades ought to be ploughed back into that sector. I give him full credit for the part he and his colleagues played in that.
Having that in mind, I was particularly saddened just the other day to hear the federal government, using the excuse of provincial jurisdiction, say that it was getting out. A great deal still has to be done, particularly at a time when we finally have some provincial governments trying to resolve with a great deal of difficulty some of the very emotional and hard nut cases of conflict over resource versus environment and other types of priorities for our forest lands.
The federal government is withdrawing from an area which everybody on both sides of those controversies and anybody connected with forestry agrees is a vital priority. One way we can try to get some of the heat of these arguments subdued is by renewing our commitment to a healthy and vital industry in which we can expect those resources to renew themselves with our assistance. Therefore, I regret that very much and hope the next government of whatever stripe will review that decision and renew what has been our commitment for the last few years to the health of that industry.
Related to that is another item which I raised briefly this morning. It has to do with the issue of tree spiking and the reluctance so far of the federal government to move in a serious way to impose penalties on those eco-terrorists. They threaten the lives of woodworkers whose job it is, whether they are in saw mills or loggers in the bush mainly on public lands and public property, to harvest our forest resource.
In saying that I recognize there are serious and in many cases valid differences of opinion as to what lands ought to be used industrially and what lands ought to be used for wildlife or other preservation or recreational opportunities. However, tree spiking is dangerous to life and is totally irresponsible. Everybody from the forest industry, the mainstream environmental organizations, government, labour and industry, agrees. For example, there is the kind of eco-terrorism Paul Watson was preaching by suggesting that some 20,000 trees in the Clayoquot Sound area had been spiked. We found
Government Orders
evidence as early as last November that many of them had been and he can get away with it.
One province, British Columbia, has legislation that tries to come to grips with that and has named it as a serious offence. Reports were emanating from the B.C. Forestry Alliance and the Council of Forest Industries that the former Minister of Justice in this House had a team working on drafting amendments to the Criminal Code to specify tree spiking as a serious criminal offence. I currently have a private member's motion on the Order Paper dealing with that same issue in that same way and asking for minimum two-year sentences for those who counsel, incite or engage in tree spiking.
It is important. We have to send a clear message that that kind of terrorism, whether it is the spiking of trees or putting bombs in mailboxes, whatever kind of terrorism we are dealing with will not be tolerated and that is the will of this place.
I urge Department of Justice officials and the new justice minister to so act as soon as possible. At least declare that is the intention of the government. Hopefully we can find the time to do it before this Parliament is ended, but at least declare we are moving in that direction.
I briefly want to mention, another area in the economic and fiscal statement of last December it was stated:
Funding of up to $90 million will be made available for projects to relieve critical bottlenecks and improve safety on highly travelled federal highways in national parks in British Columbia and Alberta. These highways are essential components of major east-west transportation corridors which are key to commerce, industry, tourism and personal travel in western Canada.
That is also a public safety issue. For years the city of Revelstoke, many others from that region and I have been urging the federal government to do some widening of the Trans-Canada Highway particularly in and around Glacier National Park with the amount of extra freight and long supertrucks on our highways. Tourist traffic has also increased by the fact that they cannot travel on VIA Rail anymore and this has only added to the congestion on those highways. It is a danger to public safety. I urge the government to ensure that there is not a political bias in terms of which national parks get that funding. Whether we are New Democrats or Tories or

whatever, if we die on a crowded highway that is burdened with heavy freight traffic we are dead.
I urge the government to move in that direction and to make that program fair. We are happy to see it. Let us make it fair; let us save lives. While that is being done some of the park maintenance budgets should be increased. Then other park services would not have to be robbed to provide minimum safety and equipment to the Parks Canada highway crews whose job it is to keep what highways we do have safe for public travel.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise today on Bill C-117. It is curious that at the start of a brand new fiscal year the government is seeking permission to borrow $31 billion.

Once again the Minister of Finance measured up to the standards of his government by bringing in a budget that does nothing to boost the economy or wipe out poverty by introducing a job creation policy.
The number of food banks in this country has increased from one in 1981 to 126 in 1988 and 292 in 1991. In the past two years, food banks have become common on campuses across Canada. Statistics Canada reported a 53 per cent increase in requests for help from food banks. In 1990, two million Canadians, including 700,000 children, had to receive assistance from food banks at least once.
What a coincidence! The Tory government has been in power since 1984.

This time the government prepared everyone for major cuts. We were expecting the axe to fall. Canadians were ready to swallow the pill but at the last moment the finance minister backed out.
What is bleak in Canada is that our ability to respond appears quite timid. We do not seem to have the will to build the kind of support framework that will be required. In the 1970s we led a government that cared
about the people, a government that cared about the future and about the lives of individual Canadians.
In 1993 there are voices suggesting that Canada be dropped from the G-7. Do you know why? Under the direction of this government our economy has shrunk to a level lower than Spain's. We are gradually losing economic clout in this world, all under the direction of the Conservatives.
The early statistics paint a very grim picture indeed. Every year this government seems to forget what is important. This is a budget of despair and nowhere does the Minister of Finance offer Canadians a light at the end of the tunnel. Nowhere in this budget does the government address the issue of jobs. Nowhere do the Conservatives even mention the need to get Canadians back to work, to get the economy going so that fewer people will rely on government hand-outs.
To quote the Leader of the Liberal party, the Minister of Finance has brought down a budget that reflects the state of the Conservative party. It has no strength, no design and no plan. The Conservative government is on its last leg and is more concerned with being re-elected then looking after the well-being of Canadians.
Once again, Canadians are being forced to make way for the political interests of a privileged few. This budget does absolutely nothing to reduce the deficit: a few minor cuts, when everyone was prepared to make sacrifices, to get rid of an increasingly crushing debt. Now we are asked to consider a bill that will let them borrow even more.
The government did not have the guts to face facts and act accordingly. Its credit card is worthless and may be withdrawn pretty soon. There is nothing in the budget to get the economy back on track and put Canadians back to work. Unemployment is up to 11 per cent, which does not include Canadians who are no longer looking for work. This is the worst performance of any G-7 country.
To make us feel better, the Minister of Finance said that in 1994 unemployment would be only 10 per cent. That's great. I am sure university graduates, young professionals and others who either cannot find jobs or have been told their jobs have been cut were impressed.
April 30, 1993

Where is the country headed with this government? So far, it has been headed straight for disaster. It is high time changes were made.

This government continues to neglect the policies that would help Canada compete. We need long-term investment in our human resources. This budget has no plans to increase investments in education, training, retraining, numeracy or literacy. The Conservatives do not even reaffirm their commitment to their centres of excellence.
One has to wonder if they care about Canadians' welfare or if they are simply letting the country fall apart while the Prime Minister is spending millions of taxpayers' dollars to travel around Europe, beating the bush for a high-paying job. I am sure the Prime Minister will not have any Canadians listed as references on his resume. I doubt anyone would give him one after what he and the Conservative Party have done to this country.
We in the Liberal Party called for programs to boost our manufacturing and natural resources sectors, a manufacturing productivity centre which would assist small and medium sized Canadian firms get more value added and more high-paying jobs out of our natural resource sector. Of course these practical programs aimed at giving Canadian firms an edge over their competitors were not addressed in this budget. Could it be because Conservatives do not know how to deal with the Liberal Party's positive suggestions?
The Minister of Finance kept repeating the phrase that there is only one taxpayer. We know this. For those of us who served on city councils we know very well the reaction of taxpayers when we are forced to increase the rates because of cuts in transfers.
Since the Conservatives have been in power they have shirked their responsibility. They have passed the buck to the provinces to pick up the slack to finance programs such as health care, education and housing. When the Conservatives cut transfers they are forcing other levels of government to do their dirty work for them.

What about the government's housing initiative? Some initiative. The federal government will not in-
Govemment Orders
crease its support for social housing through Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation and will no longer fund housing through 35-year subsidy commitments.
It also expects to save $600 million over five years.
Fortunately, funding for shelters, native housing on reserves and the integration of persons with disabilities will continue. Unfortunately, that is not enough.
The fact is that before the cuts in CMHC's social housing budget these projects reached only 6 per cent of the population. Today 15 per cent of Canadians need this kind of housing-one million Canadians-and the demand for this kind of housing is growing steadily. Is this government aware of the real needs of Canadians? Sometimes it seems so oblivious to the social and economic situation in this country that you wonder whether it is living on the same planet.

The government is also cutting back on the frequency it sends out the GST rebate cheques. So far seniors and other people with low incomes look forward to receiving their rebate cheques in order to help make ends meet. Seniors benefit from the cheques as they put them in the bank and any interest they gain helps offset the cost of the GST.
By cutting back from four cheques to two a year the Conservatives are simply picking the pockets of seniors for the spare change they will get from interest on the GST rebate cheques. It is just another example of how the government fails to understand the true needs of seniors across this country.
Since last fall I have been collecting signatures on a petition urging the government to re-examine the mechanism it uses to calculate the cost of living index for seniors.
Thousands of people in Saint-Laurent, Cartierville and Montreal signed this petition. The response from the minister of health has been a joke. The government simply does not get it. It refuses to look at this issue because it knows that an index specifically designed to look at the cost of living for seniors would show that it increases at a rate far higher than inflation.

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
Seniors want real answers from this government in terms of their problems. They want the federal government to take them seriously and not give them simple platitudes before election time.

Interestingly, at a time when the number of senior citizens is increasing and will continue to increase over the years, the Tory government has decided to reduce their chances of being heard. Is it a coincidence that the same thing is happening to the voice of the neediest in this country? Is the government afraid to face people who have some very serious demands? Is it afraid to face its failure to wipe out poverty and meet its commitment to enhancing the well-being of all Canadians?
By merging the National Advisory Council on Aging and the National Council of Welfare, the government is trying to give the impression it will save a lot of money.
We seriously question the government's judgment especially since savings will be negligible. In its 1991-92 annual report the National Advisory Council on Aging reported a budget of $396,200 and a staff of nine person-years, which represents only half the cost of the Prime Minister's farewell trip.
Both councils have always admirably represented their respective constituencies. Is that perhaps the real reason why the government insisted on this merger? Do the Conservatives really believe that the facts and the problems will go away because they gagged the poor and the elderly? This is one more example of poor judgment on the part of a government that is grinding slowly to a halt.
It is high time we had a new government that knows how to listen and how to act, after as well as before an election.

The government tries to sell a message of fiscal responsibility but with this budget and the additional borrowing we learn the deficit is absolutely out of control. In 1992-93 the deficit was supposed to have been $8 billion less than it actually was. It is over $1 billion more than he predicted it would be in last year's budget.
The minister's predictions confirm that the candidates for the leadership of the Conservative Party are completely out of touch with reality when they say they can eliminate the deficit within four or five years. If this is the case why are they not telling Canadians exactly how they are going to get rid of the deficit? Will they cancel old age security pensions? Will they cut back on UI? Will they cancel medicare? How about cutting transfer payments to the provinces even more?
The government has to be honest with Canadians. We are not buying this time. It did not tell Canadians about the GST and we are stuck with it. Canadians demand to know from the Conservative Party what it is going to do, otherwise it should call an election and give us Liberals a chance to govern. We know where we want to take this country. We know that we must get Canadians and Canada working again.

Our leader, the future hon. member for Saint-Mau-rice, is committed to controlling public spending, to suspending programs that do not directly create jobs and contributing to the economic development of this country as well as to reducing our debt in proportion of the GDP.
A Liberal government will not try to reduce inflation to zero percent by maintaining high interest rates that stifle our economy. It will find a fair balance between inflation control and economic growth by maintaining the Canadian inflation rate at a level comparable to the American rate.
We on this side of the House are committed to budgetary responsibility and to strict spending control.

Here is a suggestion of where to cut. It can eliminate the Canadian Multiculturalism Advisory Committee in the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship. It can roll back the totally ridiculous wage increases for citizenship judges and political appointees of this government.
The Conservative government loves talking about fiscal restraint and budget control but it is clear from its inability to act that it is simply not serious about cutting back in non-essential areas. Liberals understand that the only way to cut the debt is to get rid of the deficit and get
April 30, 1993

Canadians back to work. We must get them off government assistance and UI. We must put the 11 per cent of Canadians who are unemployed and the millions more who are underemployed in situations where they can maximize their contributions to Canada's economy.
Without the two-directional Liberal approach of fiscal responsibility and economic growth, any attempt to tackle Canada's economic problems will be futile.

The Conservative government has been in office for more than eight years now. For more than eight years it has been promising the moon but has reneged on its promises, budget after budget. It has been more than eight years that Canadians, who are generous by nature, have been giving it a chance. Now it is over. The country can no longer afford to be run by a wishy-washy government. Canada needs an economic plan that will stimulate growth, not promises without any concrete implications.
The Liberal Party has proposals to put on the table. It has achievable measures in the short, medium and long term to propose. The most important thing is to rebuild our national industrial base and to restore public confidence.
Our party is committed to stimulating job creation by supporting the development of an economy focused on technological progress by controlling the budget deficit and by reducing the debt. Our party is committed to working in consultation with the provinces in order to convince them to remove trade barriers.
The Liberal Party has the tools that it needs. It has the resource persons. It is ready to work with and for all Canadians. Our party is on course and will steer the country to prosperity after the next election.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the previous contributors to this debate for the information they have imparted to the House.
We are here to debate a borrowing bill which will allow the government to borrow the money to meet its requirements over the current fiscal year. I understand that if the bill is not passed rather expeditiously the government will be forced into some short-term borrow-
Govemment Orders
ing that will result in higher borrowing costs. We do not want to delay passage of this legislation any longer than necessary and force the government into the position I talked about.
There is no question in the minds of members of Parliament in this House and in the minds of Canadians that what has happened with the public debt over the last years of Tory government has been absolutely dramatic and very difficult for Canadians to understand. They know this government came to office talking in grand terms about dealing with the deficit and the debt problem that was created by the Liberals. However since it began its term of office the debt has more than doubled and this Conservative government has failed dismally in its attempts to deal with the problem of the deficit.
Its policies with respect to the debt and the deficit simply have not worked. It reminds me of a previous legislature where I sat for approximately 16 years. It had a little different approach to the way debates and discussions took place. In fact we had a sort of parting of the ways in British Columbia in the early 1980s when the Bennett government of the day decided it was going to embark on what he called the restraint program. One of his advisers was Bud Smith who may be remembered from another situation and one of his major advisers was Kim Campbell. She was one of the backroom people in Bennett's office when the restraint program was being rammed down the throats of the people of British Columbia.
When Mr. Bennett brought in this so-called restraint program he said it was absolutely necessary to cut down government expenditures and the debt. It would make sure we did not pass the debt and deficit problems on to our children so they would not be able to enjoy the kinds of programs we enjoy today at their expense.
In fact the Bennett government in British Columbia and succeeding premiers in British Columbia created more deficit and greater debt than any previous government in the history of the province largely as a result of the so-called restraint program. The restraint program was actually a cover for an ideological program that the Socreds had in mind for the government of British Columbia.

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
Essentially it was designed to diminish the ability of the government to be a large player in terms of negotiations with labour, citizens groups and corporations. Bennett systematically dismantled the power of the province and created huge debts and deficits which limited the decision-making options of British Columbia. The province ended up being a very weak force in terms of its ability to aid its people, create new programs and develop new employment and opportunities for people.
The goal of the Social Credit Party, which was essentially a coalition of Liberals and Conservatives, was essentially to weaken the government to the point where it did not pose any kind of countervailing threat to the private sector. It was very successful in doing that.
What Mike Harcourt's government is dealing with today in British Columbia is precisely the problem of trying to restore the finances of the province to health so it can deliver the kind of existing programs it is obliged to deliver as well as create new programs that voters in that province are demanding.
I see the same kind of thing happening here in Ottawa where far from setting out to reduce the debt and the deficit of this country in my view the Conservatives have actually increased the debt dramatically based on their spending history. They have increased the deficit dramatically and brought about fiscal and monetary programs that have made this government much weaker in terms of its ability to assist Canadians and play a role in the development of this country for the benefit of all Canadians. In fact this government is now obsessed with the issue of debt and deficit because of the political plan of the Conservative Party on coming to office.
Statistics Canada has provided a great learning aid for the people in this House of Commons. It did a study some time back. First of all the government tried to suppress the study. The study actually analysed the cause of the debt here in Canada.
It found that roughly 55 per cent of that debt was due to concessions to the wealthy and large corporations. These are tax concessions we are talking about and those tax concessions were made to the wealthiest of Canadians, not to the middle class and not to the lower income Canadians. These tax concessions were made, according to the Statistics Canada study, to the wealthiest people in Canada, the people who should be paying their fair share of the tax burden.
In addition the tax concessions were made to large and profitable corporations which should have been contributing positively to the revenues of the people of Canada. In fact those concessions according to Statistics Canada resulted for many years in well over 100,000 profitable corporations paying no tax at all as a result of those policies of successive Liberal and Conservative governments.
According to Statistics Canada that is where 55 per cent of the blame lies for the current debt structure that we face in this country.
Now it says about 40 per cent is due to the high interest policy which was also pursued by the two parties because they are interchangeable it seems when they get into office. The Liberals sound like New Democrats when they are in opposition. They act like Tories when they are in office. The Tories sound like Tories in opposition. They act like Tories when they get into office.
In any case what we end up with in this country, regardless of whether they wear the label Liberal or Conservative, is essentially the same political ideology in office from those two corporate sponsored political parties.
About 40 per cent of the problem with the debt we have in this country according to the Statistics Canada study is due to the high interest rate policy pursued by both Liberals and Tories in office.
It always amazes me to hear the Prime Minister talk about the interest rate levels at the time the Liberals left office, the unemployment rates when the Liberals left office and all of those problems that we were experiencing when the Liberals left office. He is responding to the criticism made by the Liberals that his government is doing precisely the same thing.
The policy pursued by both of them with respect to interest rates has caused roughly 40 per cent of the accumulated debt that we now have to deal with in Canada and that this Parliament is charged with dealing with.
Statistics Canada also pointed out that 6 per cent of the debt problem is due to program over-runs. What does this government do? Does it attack the 50 per cent
April 30, 1993

that is the problem, which is the concessions to the wealthy and the powerful and the corporations? Does it attack that which has been determined by Statistics Canada to cause 55 per cent of our debt problems? No. It increases the number of tax concessions going to corporations. It increases the problem.
Does it attack the problem of high interest rate policies? There is no question about the fact that interest rates have come down but the spreads in interest rates between ourselves and the United States and some other countries are still relatively high and are still a major cause of the problem. I do not think they are 40 per cent because of the reduction in the interest rates but they are still a major cause of the problem.
Fifty-five per cent of the problem is due to concessions to wealthy individuals, high income earners and wealthy corporations which do not pay any tax at all. Why does the government not deal with the major problems? Instead of dealing with those problems, why does the government not turn around and take a look at that 6 per cent of the responsibility and try to attack that 6 per cent which is program funding and over-runs on programming? We cannot solve the deficit problems and the debt problems in this country by dealing with the cause of 6 per cent of it. It simply does not work that way. It is an ideological problem, a blinker problem that this Conservative government has. It is unwilling to challenge the people who supported the Tories and paid their way into office. That is the rich, the powerful and the profitable corporations. They cannot deal with that 55 per cent of the problem because that is where their meal ticket is to get into this Chamber and that is why we are not dealing with the problem.
The gentleman across the way is saying:"Well, what about labour?" Labour does donate to the New Democratic Party and we are pleased to receive its donations. It supports us in large measure all across the country. I think that is because we are understood to be the party that does the most for individual Canadians and are most concerned about the problems being faced by individual Canadians, including individual workers.
The minister does bring up a problem and that is that there is a lack of national consensus in this country. Canadians from every walk of life do not agree with the
Government Orders
direction in which the government is going. There is no forum developed in order to bring those people together, in order to get them to agree and to go in the right direction.
It is interesting that just a few months ago the Canadian Centre for Labour Market Productivity looked at some countries to find out why some economies were so successful in economic good times and also in times of economic recession. It identified a number of countries. For example, it pointed to Switzerland. Switzerland has a very strong business oriented national consensus which makes it a very successful country in terms of pursuing its economic goals. It is pointed out that these are business oriented economic goals but labour, the general public, government and business all have the same view of the world and it helps them to be successful.
Australia has a different way of looking at it. When the labour government entered into an agreement with the Australian Council of Trade Unions many years ago, it set up a national consensus based on the labour accords in Australia. Because this accord turned out to be relatively successful, business, while not a signatory, went along with the agreement. As a result a government of national consensus was established in Australia which made it a relatively successful economy compared to the kind of conflicts it it had before. What is lacking in Canada is that national consensus among groups in Canada which need to be onside in order to make this economy successful. The consensus is lacking.
This government has done very little to bring it together. It is a government that has directly attacked labour. In fact, I can recall when there was a grain handlers strike in Vancouver and our members were standing up in the House asking for government assistance to resolve the grain handlers strike. Essentially the Prime Minister said to our speakers on this side of the House:"Well, you go talk to your friends in labour and get them to back off the grain handlers strike".
What struck me is not that we had friends in labour or in the grain handlers union. I do not think we would have been as successful or any more successful than anyone else in dealing with those people at that particular time. What struck me is that the government felt that it had no friends in labour and as a result there was no network upon which to develop a consensus on economic issues. I

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
think it is important that this Parliament consider that need.
When this Prime Minister first came to power in 1984 he convened a meeting representing all sectors of the Canadian economy. I recall that a number of union leaders across the country went to the meeting. I recall he even brought Bob Hawke, the Prime Minister of Australia, who had managed labour accord in Australia. I understand that he brought business people and other sectors of the economy together in the hopes of finding out if there was the basis for a national consensus in Canada. Unfortunately that conference withered on the vine. The idea seemed to flit away from the Prime Minister's mind right after the conference ended so he did not pursue this issue. The problem here is that this country, this government, this Parliament lacks a national consensus as to where we should be going as a country. A country that does not have that ends up wallowing.
What we see with this government in the last budget and in the borrowing bill is that the government has essentially given up the fight on the debt and the fight against the deficit. The government talks about the net public debt in 1997-98 being another $100 billion more than it is today, half a trillion dollars in debt. That is quite a legacy to leave for future governments and this bill is a part of the problem.
What we need is a new way of looking at these issues, of getting all parties together, getting all sectors of the economy together and addressing these issues so that the government is listening to everybody and setting up a plan that represents a consensus of the people of Canada. It has not happened to date. It is unlikely to happen under the current government. I cannot see it happening under future leaders of that party. I am just hoping that at some point in the future somebody will take the advice that has been given to us by some of the more successful economies on earth and take a look at the idea of the need for a government of national consensus around economic issues.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I simply want to make a few comments on the bill debated this afternoon, and also on the budget tabled by the Minister of Finance on Monday.
First, I want to say that I am quite aware of the fact that the Minister of Finance was faced with a difficult task when he started working on this budget. The projections on the deficit in the last budgets, not only those of the minister in 1992 but also those of his predecessor in 1991, have really been inaccurate. An enormous mistake was made in predicting the deficit for the year which just ended and also for the year which started on April 1, 1993.

The fact that it was a difficult budget to prepare in these times, however, does not excuse what I believe has been a display of incompetence and, to put it mildly, a lack of frankness in the presentation of the budget. Let me begin with the question of whether this budget was competently presented and the circumstances that have followed its presentation.
In recent weeks, amid the rhetoric of Conservative leadership candidates talking about their ability to bring down the deficit, concurrently we had the Minister of Finance talking about the great problem the deficit and the debt had created. We had the acceptance of the enormity of the fiscal calamity by governments of all political colours in Canada. We had the premier of
Government Orders
Newfoundland, Mr. Wells, having brought in a very tight fiscal budget, going to the people of Newfoundland in an election campaign and asking for their support to fight the deficit. At the same time we had the NDP governments of Ontario, Saskatchewan and British Columbia talking about the problem the deficit and the debt creates.
In this political environment the minister came forward a couple of weeks back with a document talking about the fact he was going to bring in a tough budget and there was a political acceptance of the need for such a budget. That was the climate created by the minister into which he brought the 1993 budget. He had managed to create expectations among the public, among the investment community and among international bond markets that the budget was going to be one signal that showed Canada was finally going to get its debt and deficit under control. That is what he promised.
The previous speaker or I or others of us may or may not have disagreed or agreed with whether what he was signalling to the markets was the right things to do. That is not my point here.
My point is that when a minister of finance speaks the world listens. The world, not just within Canada, has invested heavily in Canadian debt and the Canadian dollar as security. The Minister of Finance sent a signal. The signal was clear: this budget was going to bring down the deficit. That in itself accounts for what happened to the dollar following the presentation of the budget. It accounts for what happened when the Canadian Bond Rating Service downgraded the debt on Thesday. It accounts for the crisis of confidence in the government and the minister that followed the presentation of this budget. We have not had a fiasco like this since the budget leak of 1989.
The result is not neutral to Canadian taxpayers. The result has been an increase in the Bank of Canada rate on Tuesday in order to support the dollar and undisclosed spending out of the foreign exchange accounts in order to defend the dollar by the Bank of Canada or its agents. Those we will not know about until some months from now when we know what the level of foreign exchange really is. Those transactions and the rise in the bank rate are not neutral to Canadian taxpayers. The Treasury bills that turned over on Canadian government debt this week and had to be turned over at higher

April 30, 1993
Government Orders
interest rates are costing Canadian taxpayers money. The Minister of Finance is accountable for that and he should be answering for it.
I said that the budget had a lack of frankness. Some might say it was downright dishonest. I am quoting from the minister's speech, the opening lines of his budget
speech:
Today I am presenting a budget that will deliver: no new taxes; no
tax increases;
When we go through this document, for the benefit of those who do not often look at these, it is fundamental that we deal with the accounts of the government on an annual basis. We use a fiscal year that starts on April 1 and ends on March 31. It is not that complicated. We need to have some basis for comparing year to year, period to period. All the revenue projections, all the spending projections and all the deficit numbers are all done on a 12-month fiscal year basis.
When the minister says "no tax increases", does he not mean on a fiscal year basis? Would we not think when everything else in the document is based on the fiscal year that he is talking about a fiscal year when he says "no tax increases"? Apparently not. He decided to save money, save administrative costs, by taking the four GST tax rebates and combining them into two rebates. That is going to save costs a little bit, granted, because of the fact the cheques have to be printed, calculated and so on. Guess what? He is combining them so that the January cheque is combined with the April cheque and paid in April.
Let us think about that for a minute. The fiscal year end is March 31. If we take a January payment out of one fiscal year and we combine it with the April payment in the next fiscal year, what have we done? We have taken $625 million of reduced revenue-because it really nets out against the GST-and put it into the next fiscal year.
What effect does that have on the statement of accounts? It works its way through in a couple of items. It works its way into the net revenue from the GST which goes up for the fiscal year by $625 million. It works its
way into the debt financing and reduction account-that is another sham account we can talk about in a minute if we have time-for this year because it reduces the debt financing costs by $625 million.
Guess what? The minister said there were no tax increases. What has he done? He has raised the GST revenue by $625 million. How? By effectively reducing the amount paid to the poorest Canadians in the current fiscal year. If it is such a good idea to combine two quarterly payments, I have an idea for him. Why do we not move the October payment to January so that low income Canadians get their cheques in January, just after Christmas when a lot of them need it? It works the same way. The administrative costs are just as much a savings.
That whole $625 million would still be in the current fiscal year. The minister would not be able to play his little game of shifting it into next year. If I have anything to say about it, when this government is tossed out we will give that $625 million back to Canadians. If it is no tax increase what does it matter? It is all neutral, right? That is the way this government has dealt with the numbers on the books of this country since day one.
Going back to November 1984, the government came into office and delivered a financial statement. The former Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre, rose in the House and said: "Here is what we are going to cut. We are going to cut all kinds of things that those wasteful Liberals were doing. If we do not cut them, do you know what? By the end of the fiscal year the deficit will reach $34 billion, if we do not make all these cuts".
By the end of that fiscal year he had managed to run the deficit up to $38 billion with his cuts. He managed to cram every last expenditure he could get into that year. Even this week, those members were arguing that in the last year of Liberal government the deficit was $38 billion. It spent a whole portion of that in the months between September and March when it was in office. This is a budget, like so many other financial statements that have been presented by this government, that is fundamentally dishonest.
April 30, 1993

I want to raise another question. I do not know the answer to this one. I have looked at how much the government wants to borrow in this borrowing bill and it is a large amount of money. We are looking at a bill which asks for the authority to borrow $31.5 billion.
Last year we had a bill for borrowing too. In that one the government requested $24.7 billion. That is quite a large difference. What did the government have to do? Last year it had to bring in another bill which passed on February 15 for an additional $8 billion. I smell a rat here.
The House cannot sit beyond November 21, 1993. After that an election will have to be called. At least it would have to be called in order for the House to resume sitting some time within the year following. There is a lot of leeway. The House of Commons fundamentally exists to vote supply for the government, to give it the money to operate. If the government had not borrowed enough money in this bill and began to run out, it would have had to call the election early enough. We all hope the government will call it soon, but the possibility with a borrowing bill of $31.5 billion is that the House could continue until some time in 1994 with the government burning up the money it is borrowing today.
It is unfortunate that this government has not borrowed just enough money to get it through a summer election so the people of Canada can make up their minds. Then we will deal with who should be making the decisions that have to do with managing the finances of this country.
A lot of the rhetoric and discussion about debt and deficit somehow misses the point. The fact that we have a debt-deficit problem is analogous to having a high fever when suffering from a disease or illness. During a bad case of the flu one gets a fever. If the fever gets out of control the fever itself can kill. But treating the fever alone is not enough to deal with the underlying disease. The disease is what we have to try to find a cure for. It is true that when we have a high fever maybe a cold bath or drinking fluids or whatever the doctor prescribes is useful. They reduce the fever but we still need to address the illness.
I believe that the deficit we have been suffering in Canada is like a fever. A cutting of expenditures is like a cool bath. It reduces the fever and tries to address that
Government Orders
part of the problem, but the fundamental underlying disease that we are suffering from in the Canadian economy is the fact that we have been going through the last number of years of recession and low economic growth.
When we look at the government's records in terms of its spending, revenue and borrowing it is clear that we ran into problems when the revenue dropped off significantly. The revenue dropped off more rapidly than any government could have rectified by cutting expenditures.
We really had a problem of low revenue, not because tax rates where not high enough, but because the economy was not generating enough wealth. The government's share began to decline as did the private sector's share. The fundamental underlying disease we are dealing with is not the debt or the deficit but the weakness that exists in the Canadian economy itself.
That is why to look to the budget for some plan for economic growth is a search that must be performed. If we do not see a plan for where we are going to grow and where we can build the jobs that are going to generate the income that will be taxed tomorrow, then the deficit today which we know is going generate tax increases tomorrow is going to become an insurmountable problem.
Perhaps the greatest failure of this budget, even though it may be an interim budget until the government chooses a new leader, is that it lacks the plan and direction. It gives us no indication of where economic growth and prosperity is going to come from in order to address that fundamental problem which underlies the economy.
I cannot help but take the opportunity to look at that bottom line deficit projection for the five-year forecast contained in the budget and see that after five years we will continue to run a deficit of $8 billion for the year 1997-98 under this minister's plan.
It baffles me how two of his cabinet colleagues can go out on the hustings. The Minister of National Defence can claim that she can eliminate the deficit in five years and the Minister of the Environment can claim that he can eliminate the deficit in four years. The man in charge of it all, the Minister of Finance, brings in a budget that says: "Sorry, folks. After five years we still are going to be $8 billion in the hole".

April 30, 1993
Private Members' Business
Why does the Prime Minister not just stop right now and turn the whole thing over perhaps to the Minister of the Environment? I see that the four-year forecast is $14 billion. He is $14 billion better than the Minister of Finance. Why not give him that job today and let him get started at it?
