that Bill C-389, an act to amend the Criminal Code (invasion of privacy), be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to bring before Parliament a bill dealing with a matter of public concern over the last two or three years. It has been brought about by an increasing awareness on the part of the public of intrusions into their privacy and a sequence of lower court decisions that have made it apparent that section 183 of the Criminal Code, which purports to protect the telephone privacy of Canadians is no longer effective in protecting that privacy.
April 30, 1993

The bill which I present to the House would broaden the definition of a private communication as it is now defined in the Criminal Code. It will be broadened to state, and I will just quote the subsection I am dealing with here: "shall be deemed to include any oral communication or telecommunication transmitted through the facilities of a telecommunications carrier, irrespective of whether or not the transmission is both originated and received solely within Canada".
That adds to the definition of private communication and deems that every telephone conversation that takes place in Canada, whether or not it originates here, is protected by the privacy provisions of the code under the sections that prohibit wire-tapping.
This particular section of the code was enacted approximately 20 years ago because of increasing incursions into the privacy of Canadians and at that time it was simply called wire-tapping. At that time all of the normal telephone traffic in Canada and in the western world was carried by wires. At a certain point in time the telephone companies resorted to microwave transmissions to convey telephone transmissions in bulk.
Then at a later point in time we began using cellular telephones, which was radio technology. Those radio telephones, those cellular phones, use particular assigned frequencies in the frequency spectrum that is available to us in here in Canada. They are assigned in various countries around the world just as radio stations are assigned frequencies.
That is an explanation of what this bill does. The difficulty is obviously one of increasing technology. As a result of new and improved technology people who want to eavesdrop are more easily able to intercept private communications of Canadians on their cellular telephones.
This technology goes a little further. I am sure that as I speak there is another technology which we have not heard of yet. It is being used in the security and intelligence field and one day soon we will have an opportunity to read about it in Popular Science or Popular Mechanics magazine. As soon as it has become public the security and intelligence people will move on to a new technology.
Private Members' Business
I know that the technology is capable of picking up computer-stored data from outside of the building in which the computer exists. A personal computer emits rays and signals on different frequencies as it just sits there. Like a sponge we are now able to simply extract the data from the computer as it sits inside a building from a van or a car outside the building. We are playing catch-up football in this procedure in which we are trying to continue to protect the privacy of Canadians.
There were a number of Canadian cases that dealt with this right across the whole country. It was interesting to look at these cases because of the range they represented. The courts began some years ago, approximately in the late seventies, to indicate that a telephone conversation transmitted on a radio frequency might not be private as defined by the code. The code says: "In order for it to be a private communication there must be on the part of the person making the telephone call a reasonable expectation of privacy".
I would have thought that anybody making a telephone call through a telephone telecommunications carrier would have assumed that his or her phone call would have been private. The courts began back in the late seventies and into the eighties strictly interpreting the provisions of the code and saying that when people use a radio telephone there is not the reasonable expectation of privacy.
Consequently there is a big gap in the privacy protections as a result of those cases. American cases had to deal with the same issues. They came out to approximately the same meanings.
I took a different view in reading the code. I interpreted the section to cover every telephone communication so that if the person believed his or her conversation was private then it was, but the courts ruled differently.
Just shortly after I presented this bill, the government presented Bill C-109 in an attempt to redress that area of concern and other areas of concern, all of which are important. The bill has not yet completely gone through the parliamentary process but it has moved through the House process. In dealing with telephone privacy that bill deals with only two types of interception of telephone conversations.

April 30, 1993
Private Members' Business
The first type of phone call the government's bill would protect is a phone call that the interceptor intercepts for malice or for gain. The focus there is on the interceptor, on the wire-tapper.
The second kind of phone call that would be protected under the government bill is an encrypted telephone conservation. That is an encoded telephone conversation in which the signal is scrambled and then transmitted and then descrambled for the receiver of the telephone conversation.
That is all it does. All of the other cellular telephone calls that we make are certainly not encrypted. They remain unprotected.
This causes a problem for Canadians. That is the problem my bill is intended to redress. We accept now that they are not protected. The government accepts that people making or receiving telephone calls on cellular phones are not protected. Simple eavesdropping is not covered under this new government bill. It is apparently okay to eavesdrop on somebody making a phone call on a cellular phone but it is not okay to wire-tap from a wire transmission.
Apparently the only people around here these days who are protected under the new bill by means of the encrypted phone call are the ministers of the government, all of whom have encrypted conversation facilities. Government ministers are protected under the bill but ordinary Canadians are not.
The second problem is that the government says that there are too many scanners out there, too many pieces of equipment that can pick up telephone conversations. There are some 900,000 in the country. What is not being pointed out is that almost every one of them, or the vast majority, are dedicated scanners for ordinary radios, ordinary televisions and other electronic devices. They are dedicated and they are not being used for wire-tapping.
The third problem, and it is one that was pointed out just today in the lead editorial of The Toronto Star, is the inconsistency of the government's position. In its editorial The Toronto Star asks the rhetorical question: "People could be prosecuted for intercepting cellular phone conversations maliciously or for gain even though it would still be perfectly legal to eavesdrop. Does that
make any sense?" It has tapped right into part of the problem.
Another problem that evolves out of this is reflected by the U.S. response. The United States government sees the same problem but it has approached it differently. It has banned at a date in the future, some time in 1994, the import and manufacture in the United States of all radio scanners capable of picking up telephone frequencies.
Until 1994 everybody can continue to manufacture, import and use scanners, but after 1994 in theory there should be no more equipment of that nature. People cannot import it and they cannot manufacture it. All of the existing equipment will ultimately, as technology changes, become outmoded. Eventually the easy scanning will die. That is the approach that is being taken in the United States.
There is the Government of Canada's approach, which only deals with malicious and gainful interceptions or encrypted phone calls, there is the U.S. position, and then there is the simple solution offered by my bill.
I want to point out another problem at the same time. The new government bill does not address the apparent problem of an agency of the Canadian government that is currently freely intercepting all of this radio wave telephone conversation. That is the Communications Security Establishment. That agency is now doing it.
Based on the interpretation of the Criminal Code the agency would appear not to be doing anything illegal. It does not get warrants. In fact it does not even tell us what it is doing. I am making certain inferences here from information that is available to parliamentarians and to people who read the media across Canada. Under the new government bill that agency will continue to be free to intercept because it is not doing it maliciously or for gain. I do not know how it is dealing with the encrypting problem but if there is any agency in this country capable of encrypting and de-encrypting it is the Communications Security Establishment. That is its job for the Government of Canada on behalf of Canada's security agencies.
I submit to the House, that my bill addresses this problem of agencies of the government. The problem has also been addressed by the Supreme Court of Canada which says government may not wire-tap. It may not intrude on the privacy of Canadians. There are

April 30, 1993

special rules for the Government of Canada as I understand it and I am always subject to correction. The Communications Security Establishment should come forward to Parliament and explain what it is doing. It is carrying on unchecked and unregulated now by the Criminal Code and apparently even by the government's new BUI C-109.
I submit to the House that what is needed is a bUl of the nature I have proposed. The government's current proposals simply do not go far enough.
As I said earlier there is a kind of inconsistency of logic here. One of the reasons the government says it does not want to ban eavesdropping now on ordinary cellular phone calls is because there are too many people out there capable of scanning. There are too many people able to eavesdrop. I think that is what the government is saying and I quote an editorial from The Montreal Gazette which says: "It would be wrong and probably futUe to try to ban the scanners because there are so many".
If the government's logic is that it does not want to ban it because there are so many people eavesdropping already then why the heck would we bother to prohibit theft? Why would we bother to prohibit smoking marijuana? I am sure there are a lot more people committing theft in this country than there are intercepting telephone conversations. I am certain of it, although I cannot prove it. I do not know anybody who is a telephone wire-tapper. I know the odd person who has stolen and if I am correct there are people even in this House who have smoked marijuana. Admit it.
The fact that there are many people capable of scanning phone conversations and intercepting them is not a reason for not prohibiting the scanning of phone calls. The privacy of Canadians is at stake. We either have it, are entitled to it and there are laws protecting it, or we do not have it. Right now the government admits that cellular telephone users do not have the protection from ordinary public eavesdroppers or from the Communications Security Establishment, or any other outfit that wants to eavesdrop on cellular telephone conversations.
The government has said that some day in the future- and this sounds like an advertisement for a well-known electronics manufacturer whose name I will not men-

tion-and that day is not now, all or most of our telephone conversations will be encrypted. It will not be an option as it is now; it will simply be there. However it is a bit of an illusion that all telephone conversations will be encrypted and therefore protected because just as the technology of encrypting has advanced, so will the technology of eavesdropping advance.
As the parliamentary secretary for the Minister of Justice pointed out in the debate on Bill C-109, we are always playing catch-up football in this field of technology. I do not really care where the technology is. I submit to this House that the principal concern is not the technology but the privacy of Canadian telephone users.
We all remember the Wilhelmy eavesdropping incident in the province of Quebec during the Constitution negotiations. That was eavesdropping with a cellular telephone. There were others. There was a very prominent one on the west coast. Even Her Royal Highness, the Princess of Wales, was apparently eavesdropped on by means of a cellular phone interception. These all make us painfully aware that our privacy is not protected.
I want to close by highlighting that the assertions of the government that it has moved to protect telephone privacy is only partly true because it has only moved to ban the interceptors who do it maliciously or for gain. It has only been done for its ministers' encrypted telephone conversations.
I submit that does not go far enough. The government could have kept it simple. It could have kept it clean. It could have had this problem rectified with one amendment to one section of the Criminal Code. It chose not to do that. We will see where the future takes us.
This is an opportunity for the government to reconsider that. I submit that my proposal can augment and will not be inconsistent with the half-protections proposed by the government. This bill will simply augment the principle of protection of privacy as it is now in the Criminal Code.
We will close the gap. We will seal it up tight the way Canadians want it and the way they think they have it. I hope the House will look upon my bill in that way.

April 30, 1993
Private Members' Business

Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to say a few words about Bill C-389, legislation aimed at protecting the privacy of telephone conversations made using the facilities of telecommunications carriers.
This is a very short bill, so short that its purpose is not patently obvious. It consists of a single clause making two changes to the definition section of part 6 of the Criminal Code.
The substantive change is to extend the definition of private communication found in the Criminal Code to include oral and telecommunications transmitted through the facilities of a telecommunications carrier. It would also make it irrelevant that the oral or telecommunication did not both originate and end in Canada. The other change would be to add a new definition. The Criminal Code would now define a telecommunication carrier as a person who provides telecommunications services to the public.
The explanatory note indicates the purpose of the bill is to protect all telephone conversations to ensure that no telephone conversation is excluded by what is somewhat inaccurately termed as the reasonable expectation of privacy, the criterion found in the current definition of private communication. As I have already indicated, that expression is to be modified by Bill C-389.
There appears to be a misunderstanding as to what the current Criminal Code definition of private communication does. I would suggest that we need to be clear on that before we even try to consider Bill C-389.
It should be noted that it is not a reasonable expectation of privacy that is relevant in the Criminal Code definition of private communication. It is whether given the circumstances in which a communication is made, it is reasonable for the speaker to expect that the communication will not be intercepted by someone other than the intended recipient.
The notion of reasonable expectation of privacy is relevant when one considers constitutional requirements under our Charter of Rights and Freedoms. It is important that both be kept separate and apart.
Be that as it may, if the purpose of this bill is to protect all telephone conversations as it appears that is what the
sponsor of this bill seeks to do, I would have trouble supporting the approach he has chosen, even if I agreed with the premise that all telephone conversations should be protected.
The reason is that the method chosen to achieve that purpose in Bill C-389 on the one hand goes well beyond ensuring that all telephone conversations are to be protected. On the other hand it may be that some telephone conversations which should be protected and which presently are protected would be excluded.
On the first point, that this bill overshoots the mark, I would like to read the definition of telecommunication found in section 35 of the Interpretation Act. It is directly applicable to the new definition that would be created in part VI of the Criminal Code. We will note it is a very broad concept. It means:
Any transmission, emission or reception of signs, signals, writing,
images, sounds or intelligence of any nature by wire, radio, visual or
other electromagnetic system.
While we might be hard pressed to discover just what this covers, we can all readily agree that it goes beyond telephone conversations which to my mind implies two or more persons speaking to each other over the telephone. For example, in ordinary commercial radio or television transmissions, if the station was broadcasting a paid for or even a public service announcement or info program it would be captured by this overly broad concept.
Many more examples could be imagined. I suspect this was not intended. Nonetheless it would be unwise and dangerous to support this bill as presently drafted.
What would be the effect of Bill C-389 on conversations over telephone systems owned completely by nontelecommunications carriers? In-house communications are becoming more and more frequent. It may be that courts might be inclined to the view that Parliament intended only to protect calls carried by public communications companies. I would not want that result because those conversations made over systems not used to provide telecommunication services to the public are deserving of the protection of the law. I would not want new uncertainties introduced in what is already a difficult area of law.
April 30, 1993

Another undesirable result may occur. Courts might interpret the provision to restrict it to interceptions of communications while carried over the telecommunications carriers facilities. By that I mean while transmitted over the land lines or equipment belonging to the carrier and not while travelling over the air. This would create a larger loophole even if it is an unintended loophole.
I understand that just such an interpretation occurred in the United States. Its comparable legislation had to be changed to ensure that where appropriate protected communications included the radio portion of a telecommunication, that is if carried in whole or in part over the facility it would be protected even while travelling over the air.
In my view this is what we must aim for. It should not make a difference that a portion of a conversation is being carried over the airwaves. How is someone to know that the conversation is taking place over land lines only and therefore the law applies to that conversation but not if the carrier transmits parts of the conversation over the air?
Private Members' Business
I suspect the sponsor is interested in protecting the over the airwaves link, that is when using cordless phones, cellular phones or the satellite link. This is obviously a very difficult field because of changing technology among other things. This is something that would have to be carefully considered. As I have been trying to show, Bill C-389 does not appear to deal adequately with the issue.
Thus while I applaud the sentiment of this bill I cannot support it. Indeed I think a more balanced and accurate solution can be found in Bill C-109, an act to amend the Criminal Code, the Crown Liability and Proceedings Act and the Radiocommunications Act. As mentioned by our colleague, Bill C-109 is still before this House.
